2983-mark-twain-a-biography-volume-i-par:
Albert Bigelow Paine's Mark Twain: A Biography, volume one part two, covers 1866 to 1875, from lecturer to famous author. Chapters follow highway robbery, a return to the states, old friends and new plans, a new book and lecture, the first book, and the Innocents at sea and abroad. Twain meets Olivia Langdon, signs with publisher Elisha Bliss, and returns to San Francisco and Elmira.

Paine notes that the public verdict favored The Innocents Abroad over The Tramp Abroad and over any other book of travel, yet Twain still did not regard himself as a literary man. He considered himself a journalist, with ambition in newspapers rather than books. The volume shows fame arriving before the author believed in it.
3194-mark-twain-s-letters-volume-2-1867-:
Mark Twain's letters of 1867 to 1875 begin in a hotel room, with a note from the Westminster Hotel on 1 May 1867 to Bret Harte in San Francisco. Twain reports the book out and handsome, but full of damnable errors of grammar and deadly inconsistencies of spelling in the frog sketch. He had been away and never read the proofs.

That mix of triumph and grumble marks the whole volume. Fame arrives, with its misprints, and Twain writes home about both. Friends, publishers, and lecture halls crowd the letters, as the author of the jumping frog becomes a public man. The book shows a young celebrity learning the trade of being famous, in his own unguarded words.
academy-resolution-1775:
In 1775 the Royal Academy of Sciences in Paris took a firm step. The school said it would no longer read plans for perpetual motion. Such plans claimed a wheel or mill that runs for all time with no fuel. The French text prints the full terms of the ban.

The school gives hard grounds for the step. Such schemes waste the funds of poor homes, it says, and yield no gain at all. Hope of a prize kept men at the vain hunt for years. The ban marks the point where top science shut the door on the dream.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1875 the third volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica took its place in the set. The design stays fixed: every known proving symptom, arranged by remedy, with nothing left out for neatness. Allen believed a prescriber should judge the record, not an editor's summary.

Long entries let patterns surface on their own, as the same odd sign recurs across provers. Short ones show how thin some drug records still were. Either way, the volume serves the working method of the school: match the patient's signs to the fullest drug picture available, then choose.

Allen's Encyclopaedia reached Volume IV in 1875, and the archive of provings kept growing steadily. Timothy Field Allen served as gatherer rather than judge, printing proving symptoms from journals, books, and private reports alike. Each remedy entry sorts its harvest by part of the body, in the set's fixed order.

The worth of the whole set lies in that restraint. Later writers could build keynotes and guiding symptoms on ground Allen had cleared, knowing the raw record sat behind them. Volume IV, mid-set, shows the scale of his ambition: ten full volumes to hold what the world's provers had seen.
arxiv-2509-00075:
Elizabeth Aubin, Jean-Christophe Loison, Mehdi Ayouz, Joshua Forer, and Viatcheslav Kokoouline model how free electrons break apart the HNC3 molecule in 2025. In dissociative electron attachment, an electron sticks to a molecule, which then splits into a charged fragment and a neutral one. Such steps help make negative ions in the cold gas between stars.

A low-energy resonance in the collision turns bound near the molecule's resting shape and drives it to split with no barrier. The team computes the cross section and rate for the split from first principles. At room temperature the rate is high, and at cold space temperatures the route beats photon-driven attachment by a thousandfold. The result suggests this split route makes the carbon-chain negative ions seen in space.
arxiv-2509-00175:
Niraj Gohil, Alexander Franke, Nawshad Haque, and Amro M. Farid analyze green hydrogen production in Australia in 2025 across place and time. Hydrogen made by electrolysis, which splits water with electricity, can store clean energy. Its climate gain depends on when and where the power comes from, since grid carbon intensity swings by hour.

Their model aligns output with low-carbon periods on the grid, using live grid and price data from Australian sources. Hydrogen tax credits further lift cost-effectiveness in the model. A life cycle assessment framework weighs the full environmental impact. Time-aware planning could cut both emissions and cost for a key clean fuel.
arxiv-2509-00375:
Ziyi Xia, Kun Luo, Hongjin Qian, and Zheng Liu present InfoSeek in 2025, a framework to synthesize training data for Deep Research tasks. Deep Research asks a model to split a question into sub-problems, reason over many steps, and synthesize evidence from diverse sources. The authors formalize such tasks with verifiable answers as Hierarchical Constraint Satisfaction Problems.

Existing benchmarks fail to capture that complexity, and recent synthetic sets often allow shortcut reasoning, leak knowledge, or lack depth. InfoSeek uses a dual-agent system to recursively build a Research Tree from large-scale webpages. The tree structure enforces genuine multi-step depth. Better training data could lift models from fact lookup to real research work.
arxiv-2509-00675:
Dong Yang leads seven authors in total, with Yuki Saito, Takaaki Saeki, Tomoki Koriyama, Wataru Nakata, Detai Xin, and Hiroshi Saruwatari, on phrase break prediction for text-to-speech. Phrase breaks, also called phrasing, decide where a synthetic voice pauses, and in multi-speaker systems the right pauses vary by speaker.

Yang and his co-authors add speaker embeddings, numeric voice fingerprints, to the phrasing model and show those embeddings capture speaker traits from the phrasing task alone. They adapt embeddings to unseen speakers with few examples, and they pioneer phoneme-level pre-trained language models, models trained on speech sounds, for this front-end task, which boosts accuracy greatly. Objective and subjective tests confirm the gains.
arxiv-2509-01175:
Neutron stars pack more than a Sun's mass into a city-sized ball, and they can ring with waves that fade very fast. D. Dey, Jeet Amrit Pattnaik, R. N. Panda, and S. K. Patra study one such ringing pattern, the axial w-modes, in a non-rotating star. These modes arise from coupling between the star's fluid and its gravity.

The team models the star's interior with a relativistic mean field approach and tests how quarkyonic matter and fermionic dark matter change the mode frequencies. Their equation of state spans conditions from normal nuclei to extreme matter and fits known observational limits. Results show the w-modes carry useful clues about what lies inside a neutron star, making them a probe of dense matter.
arxiv-2509-02175:
Nils Hoehing leads four co-authors with RocketScience, a benchmark that exposes weak spatial understanding in vision language models. Spatial relations, like which object sits left of another, are easy for humans yet hard for current models. Their open source contrastive bench uses entirely new real world image text pairs. Relative spatial relations and object order dominate the item design.

Open and commercial frontier models alike struggle strikingly on the tasks. Reasoning models, by contrast, score surprisingly high. A disentanglement analysis splits localization skill from spatial reasoning in chain of thought models. The bottleneck proves to be spatial reasoning itself, not finding the objects. Data and code are released under an open license.
arxiv-2509-02275:
Fengyi Wang, Xiangyu Fu, Nitish Thakor, and Gordon Cheng build a soft hand in human shape that reads objects and poses by brain like signals. The human touch web fuses touch, joint sense, and heat to read objects in rich depth. Their soft hand packs mixed sensors to copy those sense types in one tool. Brain style codes turn the mixed sense data into spike trains for spiking nets.

Object reads across poses reach high truth, past past soft hand work by a clear gap. A new split neuron sharpens stuff class reads by use of live heat shifts. Mixed sense fusion proves key to the gains the hand shows. Spike based work keeps the hand lean in power as well as sharp. The work moves soft hands toward human like touch sense.
arxiv-2509-02475:
Weiliang Yao and eight co-authors wrote a 2025 condensed matter paper probing a layered magnetic material, FePSe3, with neutron scattering under strain. The material orders antiferromagnetically, with neighbouring spins opposed, in a zigzag pattern on a honeycomb lattice.

Earlier optical work had hinted at a three-state Potts nematic phase, an ordering that picks one of three directions. Under slight tensile strain, one zigzag domain faded while two grew, and spin waves dropped to lower symmetry. The broken symmetry lingered just above the ordering temperature, where static order is absent. The authors read this as direct evidence of magnetoelastic coupling, where magnetism and lattice strain drive each other. The nematic signal in excitations likely descends from the low-temperature ordered state.
arxiv-2509-02575:
Zichuan Yang wrote a 2025 solo deep learning paper proposing the Lifecycle principle, a regularisation method that switches neurons off for long stretches rather than briefly, as dropout does. Long shutdowns risk training chaos when a neuron returns with random weights.

The fix is state memory: a revived neuron gets back its last effective parameters instead of fresh random ones. That preserves what it had learned and avoids shocks to the optimisation. Theory in the paper says the method smooths the loss landscape and steers training toward flatter minima, which usually generalise better. Image classification tests show gains in accuracy and robustness. Ablation runs, which remove parts of the method, confirm that state memory carries the benefit.
arxiv-2509-02675:
Clemens Kuhlenkamp and four co-authors wrote a 2025 physics paper on superconductivity from repulsion. It reports numerical evidence that purely repulsive electron interactions can drive the effect. Their arena is a triangular lattice model. It mixes Hubbard repulsion with a Hofstadter magnetic flux pattern.

Large density matrix renormalisation runs on infinite cylinders find superconducting ground states. The states span wide doping ranges. Pair correlations grow stronger as the cylinder widens toward two dimensions. At one electron per site, the parent insulator shifts between a quantum Hall state and a chiral spin liquid. Results support the idea that closeness to that shift favours chiral superconductivity. Edge mode predictions match too. The setup may be realisable in moiré materials.
arxiv-2509-02875:
Kian Milani and 8 co-authors described a 2025 test of two linked control loops on the Arizona coronagraph bench called SCoOB. A coronagraph blocks a star's bright core so faint planets nearby can be seen. Keeping that view clear takes constant correction of bent light waves.

One loop handles slow, broad distortions using starlight the instrument throws away. The other loop, run through the science camera, carves out a dark region where a planet could stand out. The crew ran both loops together on a deformable mirror, a surface whose shape can shift in tiny steps. They held very deep contrast, meaning the star stayed strongly dimmed, even while the air disturbed the setup.
arxiv-2509-03075: Mathis Certenais, François Bodin, and Laurent Morin described a 2025 software paper on the DDF Pipeline, a tool that processes data from radio telescopes. It was first built for LOFAR, a large low-frequency array in Europe. The pipeline is also a candidate for handling data from the future Square Kilometre Array. The authors outline how the software works and present a coarse performance profile, timing its main stages to show where the computing effort goes.
arxiv-2509-03175:
Alexander Morozov and 3 co-authors gave a 2025 perspective on elastic turbulence in polymer solutions. When long, flexible molecules dissolve in a liquid, the fluid gains springy, solid-like traits. Under flow it can fall into elastic turbulence, a chaotic state driven by polymer stretching rather than by speed or inertia.

Unlike ordinary turbulence, this state appears even when inertia nearly vanishes. Experiments show it clearly, yet its mechanism stays murky. The authors build their account around two ingredients found in channel flow simulations. Narwhals are exact, long coherent flow patterns named for their shape. Blessings are patchy episodes assembled from several narwhals at once. The piece, based on a conference talk, maps the route into elastic turbulence in two and three dimensions.
arxiv-2509-03275:
Eric Frizzell and Christine Hartzell modeled how a solitary wave moving through grains can loft material at the surface in 2025. Their setting is a three-dimensional channel of randomly packed grains driven by a sustained impact from a bumpy floor. Such waves concentrate force into a sharp front as they travel.

The team predicted peak particle forces in the wavefront from material properties and impact speed. Simulated forces followed the same power-law scaling known from a simple one-dimensional chain of beads. They then quantified surface dilation, the loosening of the surface layer, across materials and gravity levels, and wrote an equation for its depth. Lunar-like grains amplified the effect most. That supports the idea that this mechanism forms the Moon's mysterious cold spots.
arxiv-2509-03375:
Martin Jirlow and 4 co-authors derived an effective Hamiltonian in 2025 for a qubit coupled to a cavity and driven off-resonantly. Such driven light-matter systems underlie quantum technologies, where atoms store and process information and mediate interactions between light modes. With several drive tones at once, existing models often fail to reproduce experimental data quantitatively.

An effective Hamiltonian is a simplified energy description that keeps the slow, important dynamics and drops fast oscillations. Their version deliberately retains slowly rotating terms that other treatments discard. In a circuit quantum electrodynamics test, the theory matched measured ac Stark shifts, the light-induced shifting of energy levels. It also captured two-mode squeezing and beam-splitting interactions. The authors offer it as a broadly applicable design tool.
arxiv-2509-03575:
In a 2025 research paper, Haoyu Hu and three co-authors examine what decides between ferromagnetism and antiferromagnetism in narrow-band materials. In ferromagnets, electron spins align one way. In antiferromagnets, nearby spins point oppositely and cancel out. Both orders appear in models with narrow energy bands, where electrons move slowly.

Building one effective spin model, the authors weigh two competing influences inside it. The non-atomic shape of the electron wavefunctions, spread across a crystal, tends to favour aligned spins. Band dispersion, the spread of allowed energies, instead promotes opposing correlations between neighbours. Their contest produces a tunable magnetic phase and a range of rich spin behaviour. The framework unites wavefunction shape, band structure, and electron correlations in a single systematic treatment.
arxiv-2509-03675:
In a 2025 research paper, J. M. Gorriz and seven co-authors focus on exploring brain MRI data through the latent space of an autoencoder, with a cautionary message. An autoencoder compresses an image into a compact latent code, then rebuilds it. Their simple convolutional model trains on segmented grey matter scans from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative.

The learned codes preserve anatomy and track clinical differences across cognitive status groups. Standard visualisation tools, including PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP, project the codes into pictures that can be inspected. A new profiling framework links latent features to regions of a standard brain atlas, combining statistical association with supervised tests. Even a minimal architecture captures patterns tied to progression toward Alzheimer's disease. A second model predicts the rebuild error from regional grey matter amounts, naming the regions behind the choices. Statistical checks back the findings.
arxiv-2509-03775:
ContraGS, a way to train three-dimensional Gaussian splatting models directly in compressed form, is what Sankeerth Durvasula and nine co-authors examine in a 2025 research paper. Gaussian splatting renders real scenes in real time from thousands of soft three-dimensional blobs. More blobs raise quality, but storing their parameters eats graphics memory and slows training and rendering.

ContraGS stores Gaussian parameter vectors in codebooks, shared compact dictionaries of typical values, throughout training itself. Codebooks were known to compress finished models well, but learning inside them was unsolved because their parameters are not differentiable. The authors recast the estimation as Bayesian inference and sample the posterior distribution with Markov chain Monte Carlo methods. Peak training memory falls by a factor of about three and a half on average. Training and rendering also speed up noticeably, while quality stays close to leading uncompressed results.
arxiv-2509-03875:
Ziyou Jiang and four co-authors' 2025 research paper takes up VulRTex, a tool for finding security vulnerabilities hiding inside open-source issue reports. Developers often disclose flaws through issue trackers, where genuine vulnerability reports sit buried among routine bugs. Human triage is slow, and attackers can exploit the gap before a dangerous report gets noticed.

Earlier automated detectors read only plain text, ignoring rich content such as screenshots and formatted code. VulRTex reasons instead. First, a large language model studies historical reports to build a database of vulnerability reasoning. For a new report, similar past cases become reasoning guidance for judging its rich text and predicting a weakness category. The evaluation covers nearly a million issue reports. Under class imbalance, VulRTex tops the best baseline on detection quality and weakness prediction, at half the running time of rival reasoning approaches. Faster recognition shrinks the window between disclosure and defence.
arxiv-2509-04275:
Lassi Paunonen and one co-author, David Seifert, prove decay rates for a broad family of damped systems in a 2025 mathematics paper. Their systems pair a linear engine with a nonlinear friction term, described abstractly through semigroups, families of evolution maps. The main result gives rational rates, meaning steady polynomial-style decay, for well-behaved solutions. Two ingredients drive the proof: a weakened observability estimate tied to the linear part, and tame conditions on the nonlinearity.

Abstract theorems then land on concrete problems. One is a vibrating string with weak nonlinear damping along its length. The other is a flexible beam carrying a mass at its tip, also nonlinearly damped. Engineers gain guaranteed fade-out speeds for such structures.
arxiv-2509-04375:
José de Brito and two co-authors extend convergence guarantees for a classic optimization method to a wider family of functions in a 2025 mathematics paper. The proximal point algorithm inches toward a minimum by repeatedly solving nearby easier problems. Quasar-convex functions curve toward their lowest point in a one-sided way, weaker than full convexity. The authors study the proximity operator for such functions and track the algorithm's step sequence.

Under plain quasar-convexity, the sequence reaches a global minimizer with a stated complexity rate. Under the strong version, convergence turns linear, far faster, with a logarithmic-style rate. Some results are new even for star-convex functions, a special case. Numerical experiments match the theory, widening the safe territory for this workhorse method.
arxiv-2509-05175:
Testing an audio algorithm in many real rooms is slow and costly, so computer models might stand in for measurements. Georg Götz, lead author with three co-authors, check that swap in a 2025 acoustics paper. They test three audio signal processing and machine learning tools. The data come from real rooms and from three different room model engines.

One engine solves the wave equation in full, while two use ray-based acoustics shortcuts. Wave-based models match the real-room scores for all three tools. Ray-based models copy the measured results less well. The authors conclude the choice of model matters when building test datasets for audio technology.
arxiv-2509-05275:
Timothy Moy builds geometric structures named after Joyce from equations on the sphere in a solo 2025 mathematics paper. The starting point is a family of meromorphic quadratic differentials, objects on the Riemann sphere with poles, linked to a classic deformation problem.

Moy studies deformations that keep a related differential equation's monodromy fixed, meaning its solutions behave the same after loops. Those deformations form the kernel of a closed two-form built from how an algebraic curve's cycles cross. From that fact he constructs Joyce structures on spaces of these differentials. For poles of odd order the result carries a complex hyper-Kähler metric with a scaling symmetry, and one example leads to the Painlevé VI equation.
arxiv-2509-05575:
A famous three-body quantum pattern is placed inside curved space-time by Yixuan Feng in a solo 2025 theoretical physics paper. Efimov states are an endless ladder of three-particle bound states with energies in a fixed ratio, first understood in flat three-dimensional space.

Feng first reproduces that flat-space derivation, then extends it to the Schwarzschild geometry around a non-rotating mass. Combining the Schrödinger equation in curved space-time gives corrections to the Efimov spectrum in weak gravity. For strong fields, a normal-coordinate expansion plus perturbation theory yields internal energy corrections. A laboratory test is proposed too, using ultra-cold atoms in optical lattices to mimic curvature effects.
arxiv-2509-06275:
From a graph and a homology basis, a triangulated homology sphere can be built, show Karim Adiprasito and three co-authors in a 2025 paper. The construction makes precise an idea of Gromov and Nabutovski. Its payoff is a translation: asymptotic questions about triangulating homology spheres become counting problems for constant-degree graphs with short homology bases.

The authors construct families of three-sphere triangulations whose dual graphs are expanders, answering a relaxed form of a question by Kalai. A counting consequence follows too. If homology sphere counts in some dimension grow faster than exponential, three-dimensional ones do as well. The paper binds combinatorics to topology through one explicit recipe.
arxiv-2509-06375:
Self-driving cars that reshape their safety margin as traffic evolves are the aim of a 2025 paper led by Fujiang Yuan with six co-authors. Classic risk fields are static and data-light but adapt poorly; game-theoretic and learning methods are conservative, heavy, or opaque. The authors' evolutionary risk potential field updates risk from historical obstacle proximity.

Each obstacle gets a risk ellipse, a collision envelope joining forward reach with sideways uncertainty. An evolution factor, computed from time to collision and a hazard time window through a sigmoid, resizes the ellipse in real time. Plugged into model predictive control, the system posts smoother trajectories, higher average speeds, and collision-free runs in comparative interactive-driving experiments.
arxiv-2509-06475:
Showing how an AI hiring tool works can make managers trust it more without understanding it better, find Yannick Kalff and Katharina Simbeck in a 2025 study. Recruiting recommenders shape who is called in, so their dashboards add more and more explanations: top features, counterfactuals, and model criteria. The authors ask how a manager's AI literacy changes what those explanations do.

In an online experiment, four hundred ten German HR managers compared plain dashboards with explained ones. Practice dashboards, they note, barely explain at all and keep the AI opaque. They raised felt helpfulness and trust among users with mid or high AI literacy, but not real understanding, and complex explanations could reduce it. Only feature overlays clearly helped high-literacy users, arguing for literacy-matched explanation design and training.
arxiv-2509-06675:
Czech parliamentary speeches are turned into a large speech corpus by Vladislav Stankov and two co-authors in a 2025 language resources paper. The new release, ParCzech4Speech, reworks an existing text corpus of parliament records. Its largest variant holds close to twenty-seven hundred hours of audio matched with official transcripts.

Recordings were aligned to transcripts automatically using WhisperX and Wav2Vec 2.0, two speech tools that pin words to sound. The pipeline pulls in more data than the earlier speech version and keeps only alignments judged reliable. Three variants are offered: sentences cut cleanly for recognition and synthesis training, unsegmented speech preserving the original flow, and raw alignments for custom refinement. Metadata from the source corpus is preserved throughout, and a permissive license covers the release through LINDAT and Hugging Face.
arxiv-2509-06875:
Made-up examples for rare classes are grown by interacting agents in a 2025 machine learning paper by Sukumar Kishanthan and one co-author. Lopsided datasets, where one class vastly outnumbers another, bias classifiers against the minority. Classic oversampling makes copies or blends with drawbacks: features are treated on their own and variety is hard to control.

Their method, AxelSMOTE, borrows Axelrod's model of cultural spread, treating data points as agents that exchange traits. Features are grouped so links between them survive, exchanges are guided by likeness, blending uses a beta distribution for realistic mixes, and a dose of variety fights overfitting. On eight lopsided datasets, the method beat leading sampling approaches while staying cheap to run. The agent picture is more than decoration: the rules for how agents interact are what generate the new minority examples.
arxiv-2509-06975:
Graph learning methods that teach themselves from unlabeled data mostly fail to transfer to new datasets, finds a 2025 benchmark study led by Yu Song, with five co-authors. Self-supervised graph methods are usually developed and tested on one dataset at a time. Their cross-dataset transfer, the skill foundation models need, was largely unexplored.

GSTBench is presented as the first systematic benchmark for that transfer. Five representative methods were pretrained at large scale on a hundred-million-paper citation graph, then evaluated across diverse target graphs under a standardized setup that isolates the pretraining objective. Surprisingly, most methods generalized poorly, some doing worse than random initialization. One masked autoencoder approach, GraphMAE, improved transfer consistently. The authors analyze what drives the difference and offer guidance for building graph methods on a pretrain-then-transfer model.
arxiv-2509-07075:
Sebastian Ratzenböck and 5 co-authors study disk streams near the Sun in a 2025 paper, the first in a series called toward the fabric of the Milky Way. A disk stream, as they use the term, is a set of stars born together and moving together, stretched into a long shape.

Working with Gaia Data Release 3 data and strong clustering tools, they examined twelve streams inside a small local volume. They then traced each stream past the edges of that volume. On average, the known membership of each stream doubled. Counting the streams gives a number density far above what N-body simulations predict, by a factor of ten to a hundred. That gap challenges current ideas about how streams are destroyed. The streams move coldly together, sit on tight lines in the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, and can stretch for several hundred parsecs.
arxiv-2509-07275:
How do people come to adopt a new technology while a charismatic rival pulls them back? Giulia Rotundo and 5 co-authors build a hybrid model for that contest in 2025. The model merges the Galam model of opinion dynamics, where group debate shifts opinions, with the Bass diffusion model, a classic curve for how products spread through a market.

The merged model runs on Barabasi-Albert networks, a network type where popular nodes attract still more links. Supporters can win over opponents for good, but a charismatic competitor can convert users back to the old technology. The team also tracks Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy, a measure of how unpredictable the system becomes over time. As the preferential attachment setting rises, meaning new nodes link more strongly to hubs, the adoption paths grow more regular and easier to foresee.
arxiv-2509-07375:
Chatbots are trained on huge amounts of personal data, including data left behind by people who have died. Elina Van Kempen, Ismat Jarin, and Chloe Georgiou examine that neglected issue in a 2025 research paper. They ask who owns a dead person's data and what privacy it deserves. The topic sits beside wider debates on data ownership, copyright, and consumer harm.

The authors propose three principles for managing post-mortem data in generative AI systems. They then review the policies of popular chatbots and the answers those chatbots give to legacy requests, such as deleting a relative's data. A systematic audit of consumer chatbots is planned as the next step. Their work gives regulators and companies a starting framework for a problem that grows as more lives are recorded online.
arxiv-2509-07475:
Language models sometimes state facts their source documents never supported, a failure called hallucination. Saumya Goswami and Siddharth Kurra present HALT-RAG in a 2025 research paper. HALT-RAG checks the outputs of retrieval-augmented generation systems, which answer questions using fetched documents. It flags statements that contradict or outrun the source text.

The system combines two ready-made inference models with light word-level signals. A small calibrated classifier, adapted per task, turns those signals into a hallucination probability. Training used a strict out-of-fold protocol to avoid leakage. On the HaluEval benchmark, scores were strong across summarization, question answering, and dialogue. Because its probabilities are well calibrated, the system can also abstain when unsure, a useful safety valve for deployed AI.
arxiv-2509-07575:
Ben Andrews and 2 co-authors give a new proof method in 2025 for global Harnack inequalities, estimates that compare a solution's values across space and time. Their target is the pointwise Harnack inequality for positive solutions of the linear Schrödinger equation on a Riemannian manifold with nonnegative Ricci curvature and a potential bounded below. Classic proofs first prove a gradient estimate, following Li and Yau, and demand very smooth solutions.

The new approach proves the inequality directly through a multi-point maximum principle, comparing the solution at several points at once. Avoiding higher-order derivatives lets the proof assume only twice-differentiable solutions. For the quadratic potential on Euclidean space, the method yields a new Harnack inequality with sharper constants. Solutions with a gradient drift term are also treated, including the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck operator used in probability.
arxiv-2509-08075:
Telling a language model to act as a persona can make it refuse harmless requests, measure Flor Miriam Plaza-del-Arco and 5 co-authors in a 2025 paper on model behaviour. Personalisation is spreading, yet recent work hinted that persona prompts raise false refusals, cases where the model wrongly declines a legitimate task. Nobody had quantified the effect properly.

Fifteen sociodemographic personas, spanning gender, race, religion, and disability, are tested across sixteen models and three tasks, with nine prompt paraphrases controlling for wording luck. The design separates genuine persona effects from noise. False refusals are not harmless: if they cluster on particular identities, personalised systems quietly give worse service to the very users they imitate.
arxiv-2509-08175:
Kensuke Akita and 2 co-authors propose a way for the early universe to hide big flavour gaps inside a zero total, in a 2025 cosmology paper. Their route uses the Affleck-Dine mechanism. In that scheme, a scalar field moves in the young universe and makes more matter than antimatter. Here the field also breaks into lumps called Q-balls.

The gaps are in lepton flavour: electrons, muons, and taus. One flavour can hold a surplus while another holds a matching deficit. The total stays zero on its own, with no fine tuning. Neutrino mixing later spreads the gaps around. That spread dodges the tight limits from the first minutes of the universe and from the microwave sky.
arxiv-2509-08675:
Liyu Zhong and 1 co-author give a fast way to build hyperuniform fields in a 2025 paper. Such fields hold down large scale swings in density, yet keep rich local disorder. That mix suits new materials for light, heat, and strength uses.

Their method shapes a field by its spectrum, the mix of wave sizes it holds. A superellipse form lets them tune round and stretched patterns on their own, with no slow loop of steps. Tests in two and three dimensions show tight control and huge speed gains. A simple cutoff step then turns fields into two phase maps for study of small scale form.
arxiv-2509-09075:
Chloe Ngo and 2 co-authors study optimal control of an SIR disease model where noncompliance spreads socially in a 2025 paper. SIR splits a population into susceptible, infected, and recovered groups. Here people also split into those who follow prevention measures and those who do not.

Noncompliance itself spreads like a contagion alongside the disease. The authors derive the reproductive ratio and analyze disease free equilibria. A policymaker can use mandates, treatment, and education campaigns as controls to minimize a cost function. Existence of optimal controls is proved for general costs. Numerical tests show how optimal strategy depends on policymaker preferences.
arxiv-2509-09175:
Fine-tuning a huge speech model to catch audio deepfakes works, but it costs a fortune in computing. Zihan Pan, Sailor Hardik Bhupendra, and Jinyang Wu propose MoLEx in a 2025 research paper. MoLEx mixes low-rank adaptation with a mixture-of-experts router inside self-supervised speech models. Only selected experts get fine-tuned for a given input, preserving the pre-trained knowledge.

During testing, the router reactivated the same experts for familiar attacks. It switched to different experts for novel spoofs, showing domain-aware adaptability. Extra experts can be trained later for new attack types without touching the whole model. On a major spoofing benchmark, MoLEx reached state-of-the-art error rates without data augmentation. As voice cloning keeps improving, detectors that adapt cheaply to each new fake may matter more than detectors that are merely strong once.
arxiv-2509-09275:
Lixing Zhang and 1 co-author present Neural Transformer Backflow for strongly correlated materials in a 2025 paper. Such materials host rich quantum phases, but strong interactions make them hard to solve. Their method is a neural trial wavefunction set in a multi-band frame.

It uses few parameters, is fermionic by build, and keeps momentum exact. That gives direct ground states at each momentum, with gaps and degeneracies in view. Small systems are solved with high accuracy, and sizes well past exact methods are reached. In twisted MoTe2, one frame captures density waves, fractional Chern insulators, and Hall fluids. A scalable route to new phases is claimed.
arxiv-2509-09675:
Runpeng Dai and 10 co-authors add curiosity to reinforcement learning for language models in a 2025 paper. Training with rewards that can be checked automatically sharpens reasoning, but models often explore too narrowly, settle early, and lose variety, a failure called entropy collapse. Their framework, CDE, pays the model a bonus for following its own curiosity instead of only chasing the reward.

Curiosity is read from two places: how perplexed the acting model is by its own reply, and how much a multi-headed value model disagrees with itself. Theory links the first bonus to punishing confident mistakes and the second to classic count-based exploration. Scores on AIME problems rose by roughly three points over standard training.
arxiv-2509-09875:
Yutaro Tanaka and 3 co-authors show that a crystal's electronic topology can sculpt the shape it grows into in a 2025 condensed matter letter. Crystal outlines are usually blamed on how material diffuses toward the growing surface. Here the driver sits inside the material itself: higher-order topological states make corners sprint ahead of face centres, hollowing the crystal into a hopper-like form through a mechanism with no diffusion-based analogue.

Comparing normal and topological crystals at equal fractal dimension under fast growth separates the two regimes cleanly. Ordinary crystals branch into dendrites, while topological ones keep the hollowed outline, marked by a smaller coastline fractal dimension. The work ties a measurable growth pattern directly to an abstract electronic phase, giving growers a new diagnostic.
arxiv-2509-10275:
I. Mariani and 7 co-authors map the jets of a black hole system with the MeerKAT radio telescope in this 2025 paper. GRS 1758-258 is an X-ray binary, a black hole feeding on a companion star. Its jets run into the gas around it and bend into a Z shape stretching across parsecs, dumping energy into the neighborhood.

Seven hours of MeerKAT observations revealed a jet and counter-jet ending in bow shocks. The two lobes differ: the northern one mixes synchrotron and thermal emission, while the southern is mostly thermal. Gas densities, lobe ages, and jet power were all estimated, and one part of the northern jet is measurably moving. The lobes look younger than those of similar systems.
arxiv-2509-10475:
Peiyan Yuan and seven co-authors design a dynamic offloading algorithm for collaborative edge computing in this 2025 study of networked servers. When edge machines share work, the gains in resource use come with a risk: queues can grow unstable. Earlier methods, the authors argue, paid too little attention to that stability side of the trade-off.

They build a multi-hop transmission model and a cost model covering energy and delay, then add a time-varying queue model to keep the system steady. On that foundation, their algorithm LDSO uses Lyapunov optimization to choose offloading decisions that lower cost while holding long-term stability. Theory and experiments both say the approach improves cost efficiency and stability over the state of the art.
arxiv-2509-10675:
Syed U. Naqvi and Chandra Kant Mishra sharpen a test of Einstein's no-hair idea in this 2025 paper. The test uses gravitational waves. A spinning object squashes under its own rotation. For black holes, the size of that squash takes a fixed value. The value is the spin-induced quadrupole moment. Measuring it in a binary's signal tests whether the objects really are black holes.

Earlier studies assumed circular orbits. Naqvi and Mishra extend the analysis to eccentric binaries. They use Fisher matrix forecasts. Take a ten-solar-mass system with fast spins. Eccentricity cuts the measurement error sharply. It falls from about eighteen percent, in the circular case, to near eight percent. A more eccentric start reaches four percent. The future Cosmic Explorer detector helps further. Eccentricity and better sensitivity together improve the test by almost tenfold.
arxiv-2509-10875:
Is thinking of AI as an agent holding the field back? Jesse Gardner and Vladimir A. Baulin argue it might be, in this 2025 position paper. The agent concept has steered artificial intelligence from its foundations to today's language model assistants. The authors find it riddled with ambiguity, and a human-shaped bias that may limit what researchers can imagine.

They sort systems into three kinds. Agentic systems are semi-autonomous and agency-flavored, like LLM agents. Agential systems are truly self-producing, which so far means only living things. Non-agentic tools show no impression of agency at all. Surveying the literature, they show autonomy and goal-directedness resist clean definition and measurement. The agentic label on language models can hide the actual computation. Their alternative looks to dynamics at the level of whole systems, to models of the world, and to material intelligence, for a less human-shaped path.
arxiv-2509-11875:
Matteo Bruno and four co-authors argue that getting around a city means three different things at once, in this 2025 urban science paper. Accessibility shapes inclusive urban design, but squeezing it into one universal metric has repeatedly limited its usefulness for measurement and governance.

Building on earlier work, the authors define accessibility through proximity, opportunity, and value. Proximity covers active, short-range access to local services; opportunity covers quick reach to non-local resources like jobs and major cultural venues; value captures the quality and personal significance of the destinations themselves. Improving all three sounds ideal, yet users and contexts force trade-offs, so a one-size-fits-all target is neither practical nor desirable. The framework is offered as a foundation for quantitative models that respect the dimensions' interactions and support comparison and decision-making across settings.
arxiv-2509-11975:
Laura Mack's 2025 paper, written with Marvin Kähnert and Norbert Pirk, tackles how land and air interact near the ground. That coupling shapes temperature profiles close to the surface, but small-scale turbulence and patchy ground make it uncertain. A probabilistic method, one that carries uncertainty openly, fits the problem well.

The team built a copula Bayesian network to fill in temperature profiles. Bayesian networks track how uncertainty spreads, and copulas describe complex links between variables. In winter tests, their method reduced a warm bias found in standard weather forecasts for stable boundary layers, the calm cold air layers near the ground. It represented cold extremes better and gave criteria for when the method should be used in forecast models.
arxiv-2509-12175:
A vibrating silicon nitride membrane inside an optical cavity doubles as an exquisitely sensitive accelerometer, and M. Dey Chowdhury with four co-authors aim it at ultralight dark matter in 2025. Such detectors can cool and read mechanical motion near the quantum limit.

The cryogenic device sits on a copper plate at four kelvin. Photothermal tuning sweeps its resonance near thirty-nine kilohertz. Feedback cooling and shot-noise-limited readout reach acceleration sensitivity around ten nano-g per root hertz nearby. Because the detector material is inhomogeneous, it can couple directly to the field's vector interaction. That field is the dark matter candidate being hunted. A matched-filter search saw no signal. The resulting bounds sit above equivalence-principle tests for now, but stable quantum-limited running points to a scalable path.
arxiv-2509-12275:
Jinghua Zhao and 6 co-authors propose Omni-CLST in a 2025 paper on audio question answering. Large audio-language models must both hear fine details and reason about them to answer questions. Earlier methods often built new datasets, while existing high-quality data stayed underused, the authors argue.

Omni-CLST uses curriculum learning, ordering training examples by difficulty based on the model's own errors. A guided selective chain-of-thought strategy focuses step-by-step reasoning on challenging cases and drops it elsewhere. Experiments reported strong accuracy on the MMAU-mini benchmark and a new state-of-the-art result on MMAR in the authors' tests. The framework shows robust generalization for multimodal audio-language understanding without relying mainly on newly constructed data.
arxiv-2509-12475:
Suk Hyun Sung and 12 co-authors demonstrate atomic imaging at very low temperature in a 2025 paper on cryogenic electron microscopy. Cooling samples below ninety kelvin can protect organic specimens from beam damage and reveal emergent electronic phases in quantum materials. Current side-entry liquid helium stages, however, lack the stability needed for the sharpest imaging.

The team reached sub-Angstrom imaging, resolution finer than the spacing of atoms, with a side-entry stage at specimen temperatures down to about twenty kelvin. They report low stage drift and stable hold times over extended periods. That combination addresses the mechanical and thermal stability problem that limited earlier designs. The result points toward next-generation cryogenic transmission electron microscopes for sensitive materials and biology.
arxiv-2509-12575:
Wei Lei and 9 co-authors model strangeness production in proton-lead collisions in a 2025 physics paper. The collisions were studied at a stated collision energy using the PACIAE model, a model run of particle production. The authors examine single- and multi-strange particles, which carry the strange quark flavor and trace how matter forms.

They test the effects of color reconnection, rope hadronization, and partonic and hadronic rescattering, varied mechanisms for how quarks and particles rearrange. Kaon production changed little under any mechanism. A quantum-based reconnection scheme enhanced baryon production but still fell short of measured strange baryon yields. Joining that scheme with flavor ropes and string shoving shown the data well. Hadronic rescattering promoted multi-strange baryon production, while partonic rescattering had a weak effect.
arxiv-2509-13375:
Yuxiao Lee, Xiaofeng Cao and four co-authors dissect in 2025 why vision-language models detect out-of-distribution inputs with no training. Zero-shot skill is vital for reliable systems, yet its drivers were murky. Single-modal rivals offer a contrast.

Embedding traits that enable detection are formalized step by step. Gains over single-modal paths trace to rich semantic novelty use. A sharp asymmetry emerges: noise resilience is strong, but prompt wording sways results heavily. Builders gain grounded guidance: guard prompts as carefully as images. Future robust designs must test both channels.
arxiv-2509-13475:
Le-Anh Nguyen and 4 co-authors probe how pairing shapes tin nuclei in a 2025 paper. For more than a decade, data on tin isotopes near mass one hundred ten have puzzled nuclear theorists. The light tin isotopes look round, yet they are soft: easy to bend out of shape. Explaining both traits at once has proved hard.

The team asks if a small boost to pairing, the force that binds like nucleons in pairs, can fix the clash. They first run a standard round-shape model to find which isotopes want to deform. They then raise the pairing strength a bit, just enough to match the known binding energy of those same isotopes. That modest change, with a fixed set of model choices, is their test of whether pairing alone can keep the nuclei round and soft at once.
arxiv-2509-13575:
Benjamin Wilfong and five co-authors describe a benchmarking tool in a 2025 supercomputing paper. New supercomputers must be tested with real application codes before scientists trust them. The Multicomponent Flow Code is a fluid dynamics solver packaged for exactly that job. Its toolchain automates setup, building, testing, and timing.

The team reports results across five generations of NVIDIA graphics processors. They also cover three generations of AMD processors and several central processor families. Compilers came from Intel, Cray, NVIDIA, AMD, and GNU. The main score is wall-clock time per grid point. Along the way the tests exposed compiler bugs and slowdowns on flagship machines. These included Frontier and El Capitan, across about fifty devices in all.
arxiv-2509-13675:
Guangqian Zhao, in a solo 2025 probability paper, builds one solution flow that works at once under a whole family of martingale laws. Robust finance and stochastic analysis often face many plausible probability models at once, with volatility bounded but not fixed, and classical solutions are built model by model.

Zhao first constructs a single causal map, built from regularized dyadic sums, that returns the quadratic variation correctly under every law in the family. For well-behaved scalar coefficients, a Lamperti change of variables turns that map into a smooth flow with the cocycle property, matching the classical Itô solution under each model. On large common sets, called capacity cores, the flow and its sensitivities stay continuous, yielding robust sensitivity formulas for payoffs.
arxiv-2509-13775:
Vani Kanjirangat, Ljiljana Dolamic, and Fabio Rinaldi compare frugal ways to identify Arabic dialects in a 2025 language technology paper. Arabic varies sharply by region, and telling dialects apart matters for downstream tools, but full fine-tuning for every variant is expensive in both data and compute.

The team tested soft-prompting methods, which train small prompt vectors instead of the whole model, including prefix-tuning, prompt-tuning, and P-tuning variants, plus LoRA, which adds small trainable matrices. They also probed large language models with zero and few examples. The big models struggled with dialect nuances when merely prompted. Soft-prompted encoders did better, and LoRA fine-tuned models did best of all, even beating full fine-tuning.
arxiv-2509-14175:
Alonso Tlali and five co-authors run a thermostatistical analysis of proton-proton collisions in a 2025 particle physics paper. They use ALICE data from the Large Hadron Collider across several collision energies. The team treat the normalized transverse momentum spectrum of produced charged particles as a probability distribution over microscopic states. That spectrum is the raw material for computing entropy and energy in a statistical mechanics style.

From it they extract entropy by Shannon's definition. Average momentum serves as an energy estimator, and temperature comes from the low-momentum slope. The spectrum is fitted with Hagedorn and Tricomi functions inside a nonextensive framework. Solving the fundamental thermodynamic relation ties the pieces into a consistent picture. The internal energy grows nonlinearly with collision energy. The effective degrees of freedom are richer than a simple count of quark flavors. The system departs from an ideal gas.
arxiv-2509-14275:
Nobin Sarwar and Shubhashis Roy Dipta present FedMentor in 2025, a private way to adapt language models for mental health work. Clinics and services hold sensitive text they cannot pool. Training must stay split across sites, yet still protect each site.

FedMentor trains across sites with federated learning, where only model updates move, not raw data. Each site adds noise scaled to how sensitive its data are, under a method called differential privacy. The server can ease noise if quality drops too far. On three mental health data sets, FedMentor raised safe output rates and lowered toxic replies. Answer quality stayed close to a non private baseline and near a centralised upper bound.
arxiv-2509-14475:
Dimitris Bertsimas and Carol Gao ask in 2025 whether matching markets should relax stability, the rule that no pair would rather break away and match elsewhere. Deferred acceptance algorithms enforce stability but ignore other goals such as travel cost or access.

Their optimisation based assignment trades a small number of blocking pairs against other objectives directly. To scale, an inverse optimisation method finds the cost vector that implicitly favours stability. Tests cover school assignment and medical residency matching, two classic deferred acceptance domains. On simulated Boston public school data, their method cut transport cost and raised the number of students receiving a listed choice. Controlled instability may buy large welfare gains where stability was treated as absolute.
arxiv-2509-14575:
Andrew Qing He and Wei Cai present a method in 2025 for solving Fokker-Planck equations, which describe how a probability distribution drifts and spreads over time. Direct solvers struggle in high dimensions. A sampler that can draw from the solution distribution is often enough.

Their weak adversarial training learns a neural pushforward map that generates the solution distribution. A weak formulation moves derivatives onto simple plane wave test functions, where they are known exactly. The problem becomes a Monte Carlo importance sampling task with a natural sampling strategy and probability conservation built in. Adversarial training pits the sampler against test functions that expose its errors. Sampling based solutions scale differently from grid based solvers for stochastic systems.
arxiv-2509-14875:
Ushasi Bhowmick and Shivam Kumaran ask how much of an orbiting object's shape can be read from its transit light curve, in a 2025 astronomy paper. When an object crosses its star, the dip in brightness forms the light curve. Many different shapes can produce nearly the same dip, so the problem is ill-posed from the start.

The authors generate a library of random two-dimensional shapes and simulate their transits with a light curve simulator. Each shape is broken into elliptical components described by Fourier coefficients, from broad outlines to fine wiggles. Neural networks then learn to predict those coefficients directly from a light curve. The networks recover the low-order components well, capturing overall shape and orientation. Fine detail remains harder, which maps the limits of shape inference from transits.
arxiv-2509-15575:
Arpita Wadhwa, Aditya Vashistha, and Mohit Jain study how culture shapes trust in health chatbots. These bots aid community health workers in poor regions. In group oriented cultures, choices are seldom made alone, so social norms may steer trust. Little was known about that link. The team test it with health workers in rural India.

Sixty one workers compared four versions of the same health content. The versions differed only in social framing: neutral, what peers do, story based identity, and authority. Story framing was liked most but bred over trust. Authority framing was liked least yet kept trust well tuned. The team advise frames that shift with context. They urge judging bots by tuned trust, not trust alone.
arxiv-2509-16175:
Deep links tie number patterns called modular forms to the shapes of spheres in stable homotopy theory. Ken Ono proves a conjecture from a program led by Behrens about when one such form can be written as a pure power of a key form called the discriminant. The rule gives a sharp cutoff based on how an index splits into parts tied to a prime.

The proof covers all primes from five up and turns the key step into a claim about special points on modular curves. At those points, a certain ratio takes only root-of-unity values. Settling the guess sharpens a bridge between two fields.
arxiv-2509-16375:
One model that can translate speech, text, or both at once would simplify language tools a great deal. Cihan Xiao and nine co-authors adapt the Whisper model with small add-on parts to form Whisper-UT, a unified translation frame. It can take speech plus source text together, using transcripts as prompts, and it decodes in two stages to lift speech translation quality.

Fine-tuning across modes and tasks improved results without needing costly three-way matched data. The adapters are light, so the frame stays efficient. Though shown on Whisper, the approach should carry to like multitask models.
arxiv-2509-16575:
Anaté K. Lakmon and Yaogan Mensah build new math spaces for quantum work in a 2025 paper. Their spaces hold operators, which are objects that act on quantum states. They focus on a class of operators with finite size in a set sense. From a Fourier method for operators, they form Sobolev spaces, a type used to study smoothness.

The paper sets out the main traits of these spaces. It then turns to equations where the unknown itself is an operator. Methods for solving such equations are worked through. The results may give quantum physics a firmer base for some of its models. They also extend tools long used for plain functions.
arxiv-2509-16675:
E. Kongkui Berinyuy and co-authors sketch a quantum device that works at high heat in a 2025 theory paper. Entanglement, a deep link between quantum parts, usually fades fast as heat rises. Their design pairs two cavities with molecules that vibrate at very high rates. A balance of gain and loss, called PT symmetry, shapes the setup.

In their model, all links between parts peak at the same sweet spot. Entanglement holds up to heat levels far above those in normal devices. Many molecules acting together boost the coupling. One-way coupling shields the links from noise. The plan is theory only, but it charts a path to tougher quantum tools.
arxiv-2509-16875:
Qishuai Wen, Zhiyuan Huang, and Chun-Guang Li make attention both clearer and cheaper in a 2025 paper. Attention lets a model weigh which inputs matter most. Its cost grows fast with input size, and its true objective is murky. The team propose a form that contracts a few key parts to summarize the whole.

Tests on visual tasks match black-box attention on scores. Their form adds clarity about what the model is doing. It also brings speed gains from the leaner design. One unified formula covers several past attention forms. Clearer, cheaper attention could help vision models run on smaller devices.
arxiv-2509-17375:
Aayush Jaiswal, Parampreet Singh, and Vipul Arora study how to pick training samples for melody estimation. Their 2025 arXiv paper works in music information retrieval, where the task is to track the main tune's pitch through a recording. Labels are costly, so active learning asks the model to name the samples it most needs.

The frame splits uncertainty into two kinds: noise in the data itself, and the model's own lack of knowledge. A model trained on one data set must then adapt to a new domain with just a few labeled samples. Experiments show the model's own knowledge gap is the more reliable guide for that adaptation. It reaches good accuracy with less labeling work than the data-noise signal needs. The finding gives music technologists a sharper rule for spending a small labeling budget.
arxiv-2509-17775:
Why do split quantum views merge into one shared world? Arda Batin Tank takes up that ask in a 2025 paper on Quantum Darwinism. In that view, a system leaves many copies of its key state in its surroundings. Tank adds a new scale based on how much useful facts each piece holds.

Runs on a mixed dephasing model show three clear trends. The count of good pieces grows fast at first, then levels off. Heat sets a hard cost: each extra bit of shared fact at least doubles the heat that must be shed. Shared fact is thus real, but capped.
arxiv-2509-17975:
Peter Majcen and 3 co-authors cut the local basis of a lattice quantum system in the best way. Their 2025 paper deals with sims of many-body quantum systems, whose state space grows huge. A smart cut must keep the key states and drop the rest, even near a phase shift.

Their cut picks basis states from the top values of a one-site density estimate. It stays sharp and stable across phases in their tests. Models checked range from wave and field theories to gauge theories in one and two dims. The cuts lower the compute cost that past best sims need.
arxiv-2509-18575:
Search engines increasingly let language models rank documents, and that opens a new attack surface. Yaoyao Qian, Yifan Zeng, Yuchao Jiang, Chelsi Jain, and Huazheng Wang name the flaw the Ranking Blind Spot in this 2025 paper. It grows from how instruction-following models handle comparisons across many documents. A crafted passage can bend the ranker's choices.

Two attack styles are shown. One hijacks the goal of the comparison; the other hijacks the standards used to judge relevance. Both aim to push a target passage to the top of the list. Tests show the attacks work across several models and ranking schemes. Content providers could use them to win exposure they did not earn. Stronger models proved more open to the attacks, not less. The authors release their code and frame the flaw as a design risk for model-based search.
arxiv-2509-18775:
A shock at one firm can ripple to suppliers, rivals, and partners. Wei-Ning Chiu, Yu-Hsiang Wang, Andy Hsiao, Yu-Shiang Huang, and Chuan-Ju Wang extract such inter-firm risk links from filings in this 2025 paper. Their source is the Form 10-K, the standard yearly risk report United States firms must file. Expert judgment has been the usual tool, but it is slow and hard to scale.

Their method fine-tunes a language encoder without labels, using time order and wording patterns in the filings. That yields a finance-specific encoder with deeper context sense. A numeric risk relation score makes each link open to inspection. Across several test settings, the method beat strong baselines. The authors release their code in public. Transparent risk maps, they argue, can sharpen portfolio and strategy choices.
arxiv-2509-18875:
Some patients are cured, and survival models that ignore that fact mislead doctors over time. Marta Cipriani, Marco Alfò, and Mirko Signorelli improve dynamic prediction for such cure models in this 2025 paper. Predictions should update as new patient measures arrive. The standard trick, carrying the last value forward, wastes most of that history and keeps stale values.

Their approach models the longitudinal measures with mixed models first. Each patient's random effects, their personal offsets, then feed a cure-aware hazard model as covariates. Wide simulations varied cure share, sample size, and data structure. The model-based route gave finer predictions than the carry-forward route. It won even on data generated to favor the rival. A kidney transplant data set illustrates the method. The authors argue patient histories deserve full use, not a single last reading.
arxiv-2509-19175:
Bruno Wiesneth and two co-authors map the motions of Cepheus OB4, a young star-forming region centered on the cluster Berkeley 59. They built a member list of about a thousand stars. The list combines optical and infrared brightness data with positions and motions from the Gaia mission's third data release. A probabilistic random forest picked candidates, refined by checking that each star's place on a diagram fits a young age.

The cluster sits about a thousand parsecs away and is roughly three million years old. Its stars expand outward in an asymmetric pattern, drifting preferentially northward, faster farther from the center. The spread of speeds exceeds what gravity alone predicts from the cluster's mass. A stellar group to the north supports the idea that star birth there was triggered by the main cluster.
arxiv-2509-19375:
When a model sorts clinical text, a sure but wrong answer can hurt a patient. Mridul Sharma and five co-authors build doubt into the answer itself. Most tricks tack a score onto a fixed guess, drawn from the model's own odds or from how often it agrees with itself. Those scores are often badly scaled, and leave no room for what a doctor believes.

Their method treats the model as a mimic. For each candidate diagnosis, it writes fake case notes for that illness. The real case is then matched against the fakes in a summary space. A sampling method weighs the candidates and yields a spread of odds, from which the pick and its doubt are read. Three versions trade cost for depth. Across three test sets and six open models, the spread split right picks from wrong ones far better than plain confidence scores.
arxiv-2509-19475:
A1689-zD1 is a galaxy seen as it was when the universe was young, bent and brightened by gravity lensing. Kirsten K. Knudsen and fourteen co-authors mapped it with the ALMA telescope array in Chile. Sharp views split the galaxy into five parts spread across a small patch of space. The parts differ in gas glow, dust, and starlight, and they show no neat spin pattern.

The whole mass is about ten times the mass seen in stars. That gap hints that dust hides most of the stars from view. Gas traits still match the patterns of nearby star-forming galaxies. The lack of spin suggests a system still being built from merging parts. It may settle into a disk galaxy later in its life.
arxiv-2509-19875:
Object detectors falter in dark scenes and heavy occlusion because pixels alone carry no scene understanding. Yunqing Hu and three co-authors let a multimodal language model whisper guidance to edge detectors. The big model writes structured scene descriptions, tuned by instruction training. An adaptive map turns that semantic guidance into parameter tweaks for the small detector on site.

A collaborative edge-cloud frame decides when cloud help is worth its cost. Easy scenes stay local and fast; hard ones call upward. The balance targets both accuracy and efficiency. Such hybrids suit cameras on tight power and bandwidth budgets. Semantic guidance may rescue detections that pure vision misses, especially where context disambiguates what a shape must be.
arxiv-2509-20075:
Stars at the Milky Way's center live fast and die young, and their chemistry records how that extreme neighborhood formed. B. Thorsbro and nine co-authors re-measure the supergiant GCIRS 22. Earlier studies reported boosted alpha elements, hinting at a peculiar enrichment history for the nuclear star cluster. New high-resolution infrared spectra, updated line lists, and scandium-based parameters set up a cleaner analysis.

Non-equilibrium corrections are applied in full for silicon and calcium. The revised abundances land near solar scale, deflating the claimed enhancement. One star cannot settle the cluster's history, but a corrected anchor point matters. The authors argue earlier discrepancies came from the modeling, not the star. Galactic center chemistry guides theories of how the Milky Way's core assembled.
arxiv-2509-20175:
Lorenzo Giusti and ten co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on coordinating artificial intelligence agents. Large fleets of agents need a way to find the right partner for each task. Their framework, Federation of Agents, replaces fixed coordination with capability-driven teamwork. Each agent advertises a machine-readable profile of its skills, costs, and limits.

Semantic routing matches tasks to agents by searching those profiles with embeddings. Agents can also split a hard task together into a graph of subtasks. Groups working on similar subtasks refine answers jointly before a final synthesis. Messages ride on a standard publish-subscribe protocol for scale. On the HealthBench evaluation, the system improved over single-model baselines by more than tenfold. Clustering helped most on complex reasoning tasks.
arxiv-2509-20275:
Three Lie algebras from distant corners of mathematics turn out to be close relatives, as Megan Howarth and Muze Ren show in a 2025 arXiv paper. One encodes double shuffle relations among multiple zeta values. Another comes from a coaction in the theory of polylogarithms. The third arose from the Kashiwara-Vergne conjecture in Lie theory.

Their main result describes the first two algebras through one shared object: the defect in Drinfeld's pentagon equation. The double shuffle algebra is pinned down by requiring certain two-variable polylogarithms to vanish completely. The coaction algebra needs the weaker vanishing of those whose second index has depth one. The authors also build explicit maps among all three algebras. One map embeds skew-symmetric elements of the double shuffle algebra into the coaction algebra. Another, under an extra condition, injects the coaction algebra into the Kashiwara-Vergne algebra.
arxiv-2509-20475:
Young stars wear their magnetism in spots, and Facundo Perez Paolino, Lynne Hillenbrand, and Jeff Bary separate spot fields from surface fields in a 2025 arXiv letter. Traditional analyses assume one field covers the whole star and return strengths that can exceed physical limits. Evidence instead points to strong fields concentrated in cool starspots. The team used high-resolution infrared spectra from the IGRINS archive.

They modeled temperature and field strength together for thirty-three young stars. The quiet surface field came out near one kilogauss at the median. Spot fields were more than twice as strong. Spots cover a large share of the visible face, from about a quarter to over eighty percent. The two-part picture dissolves the old tension with physical limits. It also enables magnetic censuses across whole young clusters.
arxiv-2509-20575:
Forecasts of the solar wind keep missing what spacecraft actually measure. Evangelia Samara and four co-authors diagnose why in a 2025 arXiv paper on time-dependent simulations. They couple a coronal model with an inner-heliosphere model and compare runs against data from Earth-orbiting craft, STEREO-A, and the Parker Solar Probe. Time-dependent runs beat steady-state ones but still mispredict badly at several locations.

Three culprits emerge. The velocity formula feeding the boundary is uncalibrated for this use. Boundary conditions are drawn too high in the corona. And active regions erupt over the Sun's east limb, unseen from Earth. Retuning the velocity relation and drawing boundary data lower, at five solar radii, improved a year of predictions. The limb problem awaits a fuller view of the Sun's far side.
arxiv-2509-20675:
Type II supernovae are common stellar explosions, but two ways of studying them often disagree. Qiliang Fang, Hiroki Nagakura, and Takashi Moriya address that tension in a 2025 paper accepted by the Astrophysical Journal. Light curve models often imply low-mass parent stars with oddly high explosion energies.

The authors add late-phase spectra, taken when the explosion has thinned out, to pin down the helium core mass of the parent star. That extra measure breaks ties between competing light curve fits. Applied to a sample of these supernovae, the method checks the energy puzzle against models where neutrinos drive the explosion. The work sharpens how explosion traits are read from light alone.
arxiv-2509-20875:
Hearing devices must lift the wearer's own voice out of surrounding noise and other talkers. Mattes Ohlenbusch, Mikolaj Kegler, and Marko Stamenovic compare two ways to do that in a 2025 paper accepted for ICASSP 2026. Both strategies give the enhancer extra context about which voice is the target.

One strategy personalizes the system with enrollment recordings of the user. The other uses in-ear microphones as auxiliary sensors. The authors evaluate both on two public datasets with different sensor arrays, probing how well each generalizes. They also propose training-time augmentations to improve robustness. The comparison matters for hearables, where single-channel methods alone struggle to tell the wearer's voice from a nearby speaker.
arxiv-2509-20975:
Choosing a treatment for one patient is a search problem where most candidate regimens can never be tested directly. Michael Yao and five co-authors use knowledgeable language models as optimizers for that search in a 2025 paper accepted for ICLR 2026. Surrogate computer models of treatment response often fail on unseen patient-treatment pairs.

The authors hypothesize that domain knowledge, from medical textbooks and biomedical knowledge graphs, gives a better signal of a treatment's promise. Their language-model optimizer proposes and refines regimens using that knowledge as guidance. The model's prior understanding substitutes for blind exploration of a faulty surrogate. At sixty-three pages, the paper develops the method in depth. The aim is personalized medicine that respects both data and established medical knowledge.
arxiv-2509-21475:
Where Ethereum validators sit on the map affects the network resilience, a 2025 paper argues. Sen Yang and 3 co-authors study geographic centralization in block building. Location shapes exposure to outages, disasters, and state intervention. It also shapes fairness in reward access. Protocols do not encode location, so clustering emerges from incentives and infrastructure.

Validators cluster along the Atlantic corridor, where latency is favourable. The authors build a formal model of positioning incentives under Ethereum design. The model captures linkage between its two block building paradigms. Strategic co location can raise expected rewards for individual validators. That same clustering can weaken resilience for the whole network. The paper gives tools to weigh that trade off. In short, where nodes sit is not a side fact. It shapes risk for the whole chain and who gets paid.
arxiv-2509-21875:
Systems that fetch documents before answering can still make things up, even when the fetched text is correct and complete. Samuel Yeh, Sharon Li, and Tanwi Mallick present LUMINA in this 2025 paper, a framework for catching such hallucinations. Earlier detectors leaned on heavy hand tuning, which limits how well they travel. The authors look instead at how a model balances two sources: the fetched context and its own stored knowledge.

LUMINA measures context use by how far apart answer patterns sit, and knowledge use by tracking how each word settles across its layers. The paper also gives a statistical way to check that these measures are sound. On standard benchmarks and four open models, LUMINA scored high and beat earlier methods of the same kind by a clear margin on one key test. It also stayed reliable when the fetched text was weaker or the models were mismatched.
arxiv-2509-22375:
George Crowley and Iñaki Esnaola prove new bounds on how far a sum can stray from its mean. Their focus is self-bounding functions, where each input can change the output by only a limited amount. Past work fixed that limit at one. The pair let the limit be any positive number, which widens the class a lot.

Using the entropy method, they bound both the high and low tails at once. The two bounds come out symmetric, a neat trait past work lacked. They also test how tight the new bounds are. The results sharpen known bounds for the older, narrower class of such functions.
arxiv-2509-22475:
Ryoto Takai proposes ion traps as sensors for very high-frequency gravitational waves. Such waves, in the megahertz range, are far above the band of current detectors. Takai studies linear Paul traps, which hold charged ions in a line. In a single-ion setup, the wave can convert to photons in a magnetic field. A two-ion setup instead uses relative motion, needs no magnets, and can separate waves from axion dark matter signals.

Entangling many vibrational qubits boosts the signal chance a lot. The gain grows with the square of the number of qubits. That scaling beats the standard quantum limit, which points to a path for sharper future sensors.
arxiv-2509-22575:
Andrea Bianchi describes free extensions of higher categories and builds a category of graph cobordisms. The starting problem is abstract: given a symmetric monoidal higher category and a space, describe what results from freely adding new top-level morphisms with set sources and targets. Bianchi develops tools to detect such free extensions in concrete cases.

The motivating case is a category of graph cobordisms between finite sets. A cobordism here is a graph that links two finite sets, in the spirit of classic work by Gersten, Culler and Vogtmann, and Hatcher and Vogtmann. He exhibits that category as an extension of finite sets by a specific list of new morphisms. The construction recovers results of Barkan and Steinebrunner and of Galatius.
arxiv-2509-22675:
Márcia Lemos-Silva, Sandra Vaz, and Delfim F. M. Torres rebuild the classic SIR epidemic model on time scales. Time scales unify discrete and continuous time, so one model can cover both step-by-step and smooth spread. The existing time-scale SIR model, they argue, is not biologically sound. Their new dynamic version fixes that flaw.

For the new model they obtain an explicit solution in closed form. They prove the extinction and disease-free states are asymptotically stable, meaning small outbreaks fade under the right conditions. They also derive necessary conditions for the infected count to behave monotonically. Examples in discrete, continuous, and quantum settings illustrate the results.
arxiv-2509-22775:
Hao Geng argues that entanglement islands need massive gravity to make sense. Islands are regions far from a black hole that still count as part of its interior for entropy accounting. Every known construction of them sits in massive gravity, and later work argued the graviton mass is no accident. It reflects the deep link between entanglement and emergent geometry, summed up as EPR equals ER.

Critics have questioned whether that link matters, by redefining islands or denying the graviton mass is physical. Geng revisits the necessity claim, starting with a two-dimensional Jackiw-Teitelboim model where energy loss ties to the mass. He then argues the general case and closes with attempts at massless islands.
arxiv-2509-22875:
Prosper Rosaire Mama Assandje, Herguey Mopeng, and Joseph Dongho study KV-Poisson structures on the plane. They sort these structures into classes and set out their main traits. They also note where the structures might be used in other fields.

The three authors prove that these structures give rise to a new cohomological invariant, a fixed quantity that helps tell structures apart. For some of the structures, they work out the matching cohomology groups in full. The paper is short and proof based, with few details given in the summary.
arxiv-2509-23075:
Tools with joints, like scissors and pliers, are hard for robot hands to work in-hand. Soofiyan Atar and 3 co-authors learn such skills with sim-to-real transfer. Contact-rich motion needs a stable grasp plus free joint movement at once. Real joints add friction, stiction, and backlash that simulators model poorly. Tactile sensing on real hands also lags the ideal.

Their recipe starts with a simulation-trained base policy. A refinement layer, learned from hardware demos, adjusts it live. It fuses touch and force signals with the policy's intent through cross-attention. Tests spanned scissors, pliers, surgical tools, and staplers, with robust transfer shown.
arxiv-2509-23175:
With thousands of web APIs on offer, picking the right one for an app mashup is a matching problem. Zishuo Xu, Yuhong Gu, and Dezhong Yao built WARBERT, a hierarchical BERT model for that task. Older methods either classify by labels or match text directly. Three flaws persist: fuzzy semantics, no progressive refinement, and slow exhaustive pairing. WARBERT splits the job into two stages.

A recall stage filters candidates fast, and a match stage refines the pairing. Dual feature fusion and attention build the semantic codes. An auxiliary task predicts mashup categories to sharpen the first stage. On ProgrammableWeb data, it beat baselines on accuracy and efficiency.
arxiv-2509-23575:
