Listening continuously with a heavy classifier wastes computation on hours of uninteresting sound. Their neuromorphic trigger is a lightweight front end. It converts audio to a spectrogram, spikes where something salient happens, and tidies the spikes into blocks. Only then does it wake the large downstream model to classify the segments worth its attention.

On an anomalous sound task, the trigger reliably picked out the relevant one-second segments on an urban sound data set. Paired with an existing classifier on a sound event benchmark, it cut the error-rate floor while slashing the arithmetic cost many times over. The savings come from not processing silence and noise at full price. Always-on listening devices are exactly where such thrift matters most.
arxiv-2606-17875:
Staykov and colleagues model hybrid stars spinning the way merger remnants actually spin, in a 2026 astrophysics paper. A hybrid star hides deconfined quark matter inside a hadronic shell, and after two neutron stars merge the remnant rotates differentially, with no single spin rate. The team uses a four-parameter rotation law that moves the fastest spin away from the center, then solves for two families of star shapes.

Their striking find is a ring configuration: in the plump quasi-toroidal family, quark matter can form a torus around the center while ordinary matter stays at the core and surface. Spin profiles remain smooth across the phase boundary in both families. As angular momentum grows, the region where such phase-transition stars exist shrinks sharply, a constraint that merger simulations and gravitational wave readings can use.
arxiv-2606-18075:
Zhong and colleagues merge two rival styles of graph-based retrieval for language models, in a 2026 paper presented at the Web Conference. Retrieval-augmented generation feeds models outside knowledge, and graph versions either center on entities, which link related facts, or on text chunks, which keep context intact. Each style retrieves alone, so the understanding that emerges only when the two fuse goes missing.

Their framework, HyGRAG, builds hierarchical summaries that genuinely integrate contextual and relational information rather than stapling the two views together. Retrieval then runs over these synthesized nodes, reaching knowledge that neither source view holds separately. The design targets multi-hop questions where the answer chain crosses documents and relationships at once. Tests against entity-centric and chunk-centric baselines show the fused summaries establish reasoning chains the rivals miss, lifting answer quality on complex knowledge questions.
arxiv-2606-18275:
De Kergariou and colleagues build a shading machine whose body is also its brain, in a 2026 paper in Nature Communications. The actuators are wood and carbon black composites that bend with temperature and humidity, assembled into a motor unit modeled on how muscle contraction is triggered. Stacked into an aperture, the unit opens and closes to control light for uses like building shading, with no separate computer directing each motion.

A neural network trained on more than three hundred fifty experimental measurements under varied conditions governs the machine. A new data-aware backpropagation method lets it predict shading responses and keep learning incrementally as the measurement database grows. The team also shows the machine can reconfigure itself to reach the same shading output under two distinct environmental conditions. It is a step toward materials that adapt like organisms rather than obeying like devices.
arxiv-2606-19075:
Cuenin and colleagues study random Schrödinger operators on closed Riemannian manifolds in 2026. The operators add an Anderson-type random potential, built from small bumps, to the Laplacian. A key question is how far its values drift from those of the pure Laplacian. Plain bounds exist, but they do not use the cancellation that randomness can provide.

The authors prove high-probability bounds showing values stay close to the Laplacian values, with a square-root gain from cancellation. The proof rests on a general principle. Randomization improves operator norm bounds for multiplier-type operators, in both discrete and continuous settings. That principle gives a reusable tool for random operators on manifolds.
arxiv-2606-19175:
Whitmeyer studies transformations of returns in the growth-optimal, or Kelly, portfolio problem in a 2026 economics paper. The Kelly investor maximizes expected log growth by choosing the share held in a risky asset over a safe one. A return transformation reshapes the gamble before that choice. The paper asks which transformations make the investor universally more conservative, in the sense of holding a safer portfolio across the relevant problem class.

The answer is sharp. A transform produces a more conservative portfolio for all cases exactly when it is concave and strictly increasing, and the ratio of return to transformed return is convex. As a corollary, the author characterizes comparative risk aversion for a rationally inattentive agent. A more risk-averse agent there is one who is sufficiently more risk averse in a classic sense. The results link return shaping and portfolio caution in one clean set of conditions.
arxiv-2606-19375:
Moon and colleagues present a physics-informed framework in 2026 for discovering yield functions in plasticity from full-field data. Finding anisotropic yield functions is hard. Yielding is not directly observed in full-field measurements, tuning can need many loading directions, and choosing an analytical form is nontrivial. The framework works without stress data, strain data, direct yield surface data, or a prescribed form for the yield function.

The yield function is identified as a constrained component inside elastoplastic stress integration, not by direct supervision in stress space. A convex neural network represents it, enforcing convexity and positive homogeneity, plus the assumed tension-compression symmetry. Training uses a differentiable stress update and a force equilibrium loss across many loading cases. Benchmarks with known yield laws test contour agreement and noise sensitivity. Learning the yield law inside the physics opens richer material models from data labs already collect.
arxiv-2606-19575:
Mats Esseldeurs, S Mathis, and L Decin revisit Earth's fate under the ageing Sun in 2026. Billions of years from now the Sun will swell through red giant and asymptotic giant branch phases. Whether the growing Sun swallows Earth depends on tides and on how much mass the giant sheds.

The team model Earth's orbit along stellar evolution tracks for a solar-mass star. Fresh tidal dissipation rules, drawn from first-principles calculations, replace older recipes. With the updated tides, Earth survives both giant phases. Older tidal recipes instead end in engulfment during the later giant phase. Slow mass loss also dooms Earth, while faster loss lets it escape. Using the observed mass loss of the giant star L2 Pup as a stand-in points to survival. The honest verdict stays open, hinging on late-stage stellar physics that remains poorly pinned down.
arxiv-2606-19875:
Hyeonguk Bahk leads a fifteen-author validation of the SPHEREx photometry pipeline for galaxy clusters in 2026. SPHEREx will survey the sky in near-infrared light from space. Cluster science needs its brightness measures checked for extended sources before launch data flow.

Eight galaxy clusters span redshifts from near zero to just past one. Mock SPHEREx views are generated with the mission's sky simulator from DESI Legacy and COSMOS data. Forced photometry with The Tractor then measures the fake images end to end. Photometry proves broadly unbiased overall. Source blending drives the worst outliers, above all when neighbours rival the target's flux. Members are detected several magnitudes fainter than each cluster's brightest galaxy nearby, but barely deeper at high redshift. Cluster redshifts recover with tiny bias and scatter at low redshift, meeting cosmology needs.
arxiv-2606-20375:
Frederick Reiber, Alishah Chator, Dana Calacci, and Allison McDonald study how American labor unions organize through chat platforms. Their 2026 paper, published in a human-computer interaction journal, draws on seventeen qualitative interviews with workers in various unions. A dispersed workforce makes digital tools, Discord, WhatsApp, and Slack among them, essential for bridging distance and schedules. The authors examine what these platforms make possible, and what new problems they create.

Digital tools proved integral to recent organizing successes, yet they introduce their own complexities. Organizers must navigate technical security against employer surveillance, manage information overload across busy channels, and build trust that face-to-face organizing once supplied. The lesson is double-edged: the same platforms that let a scattered workforce coordinate also expose it, so organizing craft now includes digital hygiene as a core skill.
arxiv-2606-20975:
Clelia Altomonte and Malcolm Fairbairn develop a quantum algorithm in 2026 for solving Einstein's field equations on a digital quantum computer. Classical codes evolve black hole spacetimes at large cost. Their proof-of-principle algorithm uses a tetrad form of numerical relativity.

The algorithm is programmed with Qiskit tools. It is run on classical simulators and on physical IBM quantum computers through a national access program. A Schwarzschild black hole spacetime is evolved. Perturbing it yields gravitational quasinormal modes, the ringing tones of the black hole. Computational resources and runtime are quantified. A working demonstration, even at small scale, maps what quantum hardware must achieve before real-size relativity problems become feasible.
arxiv-2606-21575:
Louis Shuo Wang, Jiguang Yu, and Ye Liang solve an optimal stopping problem in 2026 where the payoff has a kink, a nonsmooth corner that breaks standard free-boundary methods. The setting is a two-dimensional diffusion reflected at the axes of the quadrant, stopped for a payoff equal to the larger of two scaled coordinates. Their novelty is a measure-valued formulation: the stopping gain becomes a signed Radon measure whose singular part lives exactly on the kink diagonal, and that part is computed explicitly.

With it, the value function takes a killed-resolvent form, where the diffusion is stopped on entering the stopping set, correcting a commonly used but generally invalid unrestricted formula. Under stated monotonicity assumptions, the stopping set has epigraph form and its boundary is pinned down by a trace condition. A verification theorem certifies candidate boundaries.
arxiv-2606-21675:
Bruno Laburthe-Tolra, Martin Robert-de-Saint-Vincent, and Benjamin Pasquiou examine the dark side of a promising clock laser in 2026. A continuous superradiant laser, where a steady beam of excited atoms crosses a high-finesse cavity, has been proposed as an active optical clock whose frequency is set by atoms, not mirrors. The authors ask whether its intensity is actually stable.

It need not be: the laser can go unstable and turn chaotic. They derive an analytic criterion showing the instability requires cavity photons to die much faster than the atoms. That condition sharpens the design rules for using such lasers as frequency references, and clarifies what the instability does to intensity noise and linewidth. In the unstable regime the device doubles as a chaos laboratory, with a mean-field map to fluid turbulence, plus a regular self-pulsing regime at large atom numbers.
arxiv-2606-21775:
Tianqi Du, Qi Zhang, Yifei Wang, and Yisen Wang argue in 2026 that world models should learn to see more than one step ahead. Latent world models in the JEPA style predict future states in a compact representation space. But they train on single transitions and must chain predictions at planning time, compounding errors exactly where planning needs accuracy most. Their Variable-length Latent World Models instead train on action sequences of many lengths directly.

One predictor then evaluates plans over different horizons natively. A curriculum that progressively stretches the action horizon stabilizes training from short-range dynamics to long-range prediction. Planning methods tailored to the variable-length ability exploit it at test time. On long-horizon control tasks, the models beat the state-of-the-art LeWM baseline by 13 percent on average, with the largest gains where extended planning matters most.
arxiv-2606-22175:
Phung and Thain present StickyInvoc in 2026, a new task model for high-throughput workflows that call large language models. The traditional task model isolates each task, so every inference task reloads multi-gigabyte model parameters from storage into GPU memory and destroys them at exit. At thousands of tasks, that create-destroy overhead becomes a serious barrier.

StickyInvoc splits the work between two task types. A sticky task builds a persistent, inheritable state on a compute node from a user template, but does no computing itself. Invocation tasks then inherit that state, compute, and leave it intact for the next task. Rewriting a claim verification workflow of 150 thousand inferences in this paradigm gave a 3.6-fold speedup on twenty GPUs. Scaling out to 186 otherwise idle GPUs finished the workflow in 784 seconds.
arxiv-2606-22375:
Yi Cao and five colleagues presented ARIA at the 2026 KDD conference. Their subject is trustworthy materials discovery with large language models. Such models can propose new materials, yet their suggestions often ignore physical causality, the real cause-and-effect chain behind a material's behaviour.

The team identifies a failure they call contextual tunneling, where a model clings to narrow retrieved evidence and suppresses broader physical reasoning. ARIA routes each query through three tiers, using direct causal reasoning when a full process-structure-property chain exists. For sparse or novel systems it transfers knowledge by physical analogy, and it falls back on its own knowledge when evidence runs out. On a knowledge graph holding 2,839 extracted relations, ARIA beat plain and naively augmented models on prediction and inverse design tasks for two-dimensional materials. It also left auditable causal traces behind each answer.
arxiv-2606-22775:
Zhewen Hou and Tian Zheng study regression when deployment data differ from training data, in this 2026 statistics paper. Often something about the target setting is known in advance: population averages, boundary conditions, or simulator settings. That knowledge describes the target distributions of both inputs and response, and it could sharpen estimates if used well.

The authors take a hybrid-loss estimator, which uses both target marginals, as the benchmark method. Computing it directly means solving a coupled nonlinear problem that grows expensive at scale. They develop two cheaper alternatives: a constrained moment-matching estimator, and a two-stage estimator that adds a calibration step to ordinary least squares. For all three they derive exact asymptotic error formulas and map where the cheap versions match the benchmark. In simulations across three shift regimes, the two-stage estimator nearly matched the benchmark when the signal was strong, at almost no extra cost.
arxiv-2606-22875:
Wenlong Cheng, Yuan Gan, Yunqiu Xu, and Jiaxu Miao protect federated diffusion models from theft in this 2026 paper. Federated learning trains a shared model across participants, which means handing the global model to every client. A malicious client could resell or redistribute it. Existing watermarking can verify ownership but cannot trace a leak to the client responsible, and watermarks stored in the model's decoder can be removed by swapping in a clean decoder.

Their framework, FedOT, uses a chunked watermark: one part verifies ownership, the other identifies the client. A latent vector transformation step ties the model's two latent spaces together, so replacing the decoder to strip the watermark badly degrades image quality and makes the model unusable. In experiments, FedOT performed strongly on both ownership verification and leakage tracing. The authors present it as the first framework to do both jobs for federated latent diffusion models.
arxiv-2606-22975:
Yeongho Kim, Yeonje Choi, and Kijung Shin compress training data for text-attributed graphs in a 2026 paper. Such graphs link items with both connections and written text, like papers tied by citations and abstracts. Learning on them usually pairs a language model with a graph neural network. Training that pair together is costly and hard to scale. Dataset distillation instead builds a tiny synthetic dataset that teaches almost as well as the full one.

Kim and colleagues propose TaLK, which couples the language model to a graph-aware kernel rather than retraining the full pair repeatedly. The kernel captures how training points influence each other through the graph. Because the costly joint training is avoided, distillation runs far more cheaply. On several benchmark graphs, TaLK beat earlier methods. It reached up to ninety-seven percent of full-data performance using only one percent synthetic data.
arxiv-2606-23175:
Steven Young Eulig argues that AI scientist systems must be judged on more than final answers in a 2026 position paper. Such systems are cast as tools, co-authors, or founders of discoveries. Eulig proposes scoring three things separately: task outcome, mechanism fidelity, and epistemic honesty. His evidence comes from twenty-eight episodes where a coding agent tried to rediscover a known observable for particle identification in a physics simulation. A smaller probe repeated the test across two more frontier models.

Eulig documents episodes where agents reached right-looking results through wrong reasoning that breaks when conditions shift. He names it Correct Answer, Wrong Mechanism. Honesty and mechanism fidelity can split within one run: agents rejected a false hint on evidence, yet one defended its observable with physics its own data contradicted. A one-step regime-shift check flags the over-general cases, and a companion recomputation catches the rest.
arxiv-2606-23275:
Zhi Cao, Haiyan Zheng, and Pavel Mozgunov design dose-finding for basket cancer trials in a 2026 biostatistics paper. Modern early oncology trials seek an optimal biological dose, not merely the highest tolerated one. For targeted drugs and immunotherapies, benefit can plateau before toxicity becomes unacceptable. Basket trials run several disease or biomarker subtrials under one protocol, and each subtrial may need its own best dose. Pooling everything into one dose would miss those differences. Their design lets each subtrial select its dose while borrowing strength cautiously from the others.

Cao and colleagues model toxicity with a monotone logistic curve and efficacy with a flexible quadratic dose-response curve. Mixture priors let the borrowing strength adapt to how similar subtrials look. Dose choices come from an admissible set set by safety and futility rules, ranked by a utility combining toxicity and efficacy. Large simulations check the design's operating behavior.
arxiv-2606-23375:
Arthur Wuhrmann and colleagues measure over-alignment in language models used by courts in a 2026 paper. Switzerland's Federal Supreme Court runs small local models for draft translations and short summaries across four official languages. Criminal law breaks that workflow. Case files routinely describe violent and sexual offenses in full, and model guardrails refuse or attach disclaimers to legitimate work. The authors call this over-alignment. They build TF-RefusalBench, a benchmark of over five thousand prompts in French, German, Italian, and English drawn from public rulings, covering translation and summary tasks likely to trigger refusal.

Wuhrmann and colleagues find over-alignment depends on the model, the prompt, and the languages involved. Disclaimers also harm task faithfulness, so counting refusals alone understates the damage. Prompting helps somewhat, while a technique that removes the refusal direction works better for enabling on-premises criminal law use.
arxiv-2606-23575:
Bay and Yearick show that the key tuning knob of spline regression can be computed directly instead of searched, in a 2026 paper on statistical learning. Spline regression fits smooth curves built from pieces, and its resolution setting controls how wiggly the curve may be. Standard practice tries every grid value and keeps the winner by cross validation, wasting computation.

Classical approximation theory pins down how bias shrinks as resolution grows, at exactly the best rate any linear method can reach for the smoothness class. A shortcut identity also gives the leave one out error of a fit from that single fit alone. Balancing the two known curves yields the best resolution in closed form. Their algorithm, KORE, needs only about a dozen fits, yet matches full grid searches while fitting roughly eight times fewer models.
arxiv-2606-23875:
Thapa and Staab give database queries the power to invent answers with a language model, without giving up the formal semantics that make queries analyzable, in a 2026 paper on database theory. SPARQL is the standard language for querying RDF knowledge graphs, and its semantics assume a fixed dataset. Applications increasingly want generated values produced on demand by a language model. Current practice bolts such calls on as external procedures, outside the algebra, so equivalence and termination questions go unanswered.

The authors add a generative operator, GenOp, whose evaluation calls a model and returns typed solution mappings, while the graph stays fixed. A compatibility relation generalizes equality to allow similarity based matching. Under bounded deterministic generation, tame fragments get fixpoint semantics, equivalence and rewrite rules are established, and query complexity matches standard SPARQL.
arxiv-2606-23975:
Achilleos and Kyriakou link two fields that rarely meet. One is topology, the study of spaces and nearness. The other is formal verification, the checking of how computer systems behave. A monitor can only watch a finite slice of behaviour. So the pair ask which traits can be checked from such short watches. Their 2026 work starts with trace-based topologies. In that view, a watch records just the sequences of actions a process can perform.

Finite trace watches turn out to generate the Cantor topology on infinite action sequences. If full trace inclusion is demanded instead, the topology is discrete. For general process spaces, simulation watches give a strictly finer topology than trace watches. A broad theorem then states a clean match. The open sets in any such topology are just the traits those watches can verify. With stronger relations, finite-depth bisimulation gives a genuinely different topology.
arxiv-2606-24175:
Sun and colleagues make fine-tuning of point cloud video models cheaper in three currencies at once: labelled data, trainable parameters, and memory. Point cloud videos record three-dimensional scenes over time. Adapting foundation models to them usually demands costly annotation and heavy fine-tuning. Their 2026 framework, PoinTriE, instead mines richer supervision from data that already exists.

For pretraining, fake motion paths are synthesised by rigidly transforming the clouds. Text descriptions and flat projections are derived from the raw data as extra training signals. A geometric-motion duality network learns through multimodal contrastive training, rotation prediction, and motion distribution matching. That yields dense self-supervision with no hand labels. During fine-tuning the pretrained backbone stays frozen. Only a light spatio-temporal side network, built with low-rank adapters, updates. Sun's team reports the mix excelling on all three efficiency axes, against existing parameter-efficient methods.
arxiv-2606-24575:
Yamazaki and Garrido-Lestache Belinchon test whether Benjamin Graham's old value investing rules can discipline modern stock picking. Machine learning models hunting market patterns often memorise short term noise instead of durable value. The pair writes from the Milwaukee School of Engineering in 2026. They treat Graham's classic screening rules as a low pass filter, and build three feature sets: pure Graham rules, modern market factors, and a combination.

Complex models, including XGBoost and AutoGluon, train on twenty years of S&P 500 data, then run a strict buy and hold over a four year test window ending in March 2026. Complexity does not win. The AutoGluon model posts high returns. It suffers a steep drawdown, though, after loading up on volatile technology stocks before a crash. A pure Graham random forest achieves the highest return, with much less risk. The moral is restraint: simple rules still filter noise that sophisticated models chase.
arxiv-2606-24675:
Codaline Bourotte, Gwendal Ducloz, Pekka Orponen, and Shinnosuke Seki introduce a new graph parameter called the KLX number. It measures congestion during depth first search, the classic method that dives along one path before backtracking. For a given graph, the KLX number is the smallest possible worst case count of back edges open at once. The idea grew out of a problem in RNA nanostructure design.

Bourotte and colleagues fully characterise graphs with KLX number zero, one, and two. They give linear time recognition algorithms for those cases. They also bound tree width by the KLX number plus one. For any fixed bound k, the property of having KLX number at most k can be expressed in monadic second order logic. Combined with the tree width bound, that yields linear time tests for every constant k. The parameter thus ties a search order notion to classic width measures.
arxiv-2606-24975:
Mahesh Godavarti explains why one kind of attention extrapolates to longer contexts than it was trained on. PaTH Attention replaced the fixed rotations of rotary position embeddings with accumulated, data dependent Householder reflections. It extrapolated strongly, then degraded at extreme lengths. Godavarti asks whether that pattern needs Householder structure. A variant keeps the rotary blocks but lets the angles accumulate from the tokens. It behaves the same way: better extrapolation, then degradation.

He proves the effect for accumulated orthogonal maps under mild conditions. Their products turn incoherent after finitely many steps, muting attention to tokens. A stylised model makes the mechanism concrete. The accumulated turns create a mixing window that does not grow with context length. The muting learned in training carries unchanged to any test length. A lower bound shows the degradation cannot be fixed. As context grows, no choice of turns can guarantee the target signal survives.
arxiv-2606-25275:
Predicting how stiff a rock is from a three dimensional scan normally requires heavy numerical simulation on every voxel. Hanfeng Zhai, Rasool Ahmad, Tapan Mukerji, and Wei Cai speed that up in 2026 by splitting the job into two levels. A large scan is cut into subcubes, and a lightweight convolutional network predicts each subcube's elastic moduli in place of the costly simulation. A classical upscaling scheme, hierarchical homogenization, then combines the pieces into whole rock values.

Three choices of training target were compared, from full stiffness tensors down to normalised factors bounded by known physical limits. All three matched direct simulation closely across several rock types while cutting computation sharply. The normalised target gave the best balance of speed, accuracy, and guaranteed physical consistency, and training fresh for each rock type was fast enough that transfer learning was not needed.
arxiv-2606-25475:
Symbolic dynamics studies infinite symbol streams cut by rules, and a classic theorem of Krieger says exactly when one rule system can be embedded inside a mixing shift of finite type. Brian Marcus, Tom Meyerovitch, and Chengyu Wu extend that result in 2026 to a broader target class, near Markov sofic shifts. Sofic shifts are the labelled projections of finite type systems, and the plain theorem fails for them, as a simple even shift example shows. Near Markov shifts form a special, well behaved subclass defined without reference to any presentation.

Generalised Krieger conditions, comparing entropy and periodic point counts, become necessary and sufficient for embedding into such targets. When the system being embedded is itself irreducible and sofic, the conditions can be checked by a finite procedure. The work is dedicated to Benjamin Weiss, who discovered sofic shifts, on his eighty fifth birthday.
arxiv-2606-25675:
Pluto's air is a whisper, a nitrogen film a million times thinner than Earth's, held up by ice evaporating from the surface. Amanda Sickafoose leads a large team reporting in 2026 on ten stellar occultations watched between twenty seventeen and twenty twenty three. As Pluto's shadow crossed distant stars, the dimming traced its atmosphere. Four events caught several chords across the disk; six came from single sites. Earlier claims had pressure climbing steadily until twenty sixteen, then perhaps freezing out.

Pressure instead held a plateau from the New Horizons flyby in twenty fifteen through about twenty twenty one, then began to fall. The clear air reading at one height dropped by several percent into twenty twenty two. A lower, haze affected measure fell by roughly a sixth. Lower atmosphere light curves changed slope, consistent with haze settling over a year or less. One curve's spikes hint at buoyancy waves.
arxiv-2606-26075:
Suman Saha leads a team observing LTT9779b, the only known ultra-hot Neptune. The planet sits deep in the Neptunian desert, a zone where such worlds are scarce. Its dayside reflects far more light than expected. Clouds or extreme metal enrichment could explain the shine. James Webb Space Telescope instruments settle the question. Near-infrared spectra from NIRISS and NIRSpec cover the dayside at high signal quality.

Clouds win the argument. The spectra show dayside clouds at three-to-five sigma significance. Strong evidence points to silicate condensate, magnesium silicate. The detection is the first solid one for a Neptunian-mass planet's dayside. A reflective cloud deck, not a metal-choked atmosphere, explains the high albedo. Carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide both appear robustly in retrievals. The carbon-to-oxygen ratio lands just under one, matching ultra-hot Jupiters. Sequestered oxygen in condensates may drive that shared pattern.
arxiv-2606-26175:
Anıl Can Ateş, Orhan Kahraman, and Cihan Topal split robot rewards into micro-tasks to speed up learning. Reinforcement learning for manipulation needs dense reward signals. Hand-built rewards are fragile, and human demonstrations cost dearly. Vision-language models can judge progress from a text prompt, for free. One global prompt proves too coarse, though. During long tasks its reward stays nearly flat, hiding early progress from the learner.

RMTL describes the job as a handful of language-labelled micro-tasks. The active micro-task's prompt scores each step, averaged over several camera views to dodge occlusions. A reverse curriculum starts the agent near success and walks the start point backward. First a fixed distance rule picks the active micro-task. A learned manager later replaces the rule, making phase selection itself learned. On the Fetch environment, the split rewards teach faster than single-prompt rewards.
arxiv-2606-26275:
Domingos Salazar proves a bounded-treewidth criterion for a question of Scott and Sokal about spanning-tree polynomials. The spanning-tree polynomial tallies every way to wire a graph into a tree. Scott and Sokal asked which graphs make inverse powers of that polynomial completely monotone, a strong smoothness property. Salazar's answer ties the property to treewidth, a measure of how tree-like a graph is.

Graphs of treewidth at most k pass the test for every exponent above a threshold set by k. Partial three-trees are covered across the first open interval Scott and Sokal left, including Apollonian networks and small named graphs. The proof mixes Riesz and Wishart integrals, star-mesh elimination, and a Gaussian kernel, building a Laplace representation that survives graph surgery. The manuscript discloses development assistance from an AI research workflow. Treewidth four is where the method's boundary sits, flagged honestly in the paper.
arxiv-2606-26375:
Hugo Esquivel, Kabir Oluwatobi Idowu, and Guang Lin address the stochastic eigenproblem. It asks for the natural vibration values of a system with partly random properties. Engineers rely on such problems when judging design reliability under uncertainty. Existing solvers can converge slowly. They can also cost too much computing time. The authors look for a faster route.

Their method pairs two tools. Spectral chaos represents random quantities as sums of polynomial terms. Halley's method is a root-finding algorithm famous for cubic convergence. Cubic convergence means the error shrinks extremely fast near an answer. The authors argue no higher-order method of that family can beat this rate here. They support the claim with error analysis and a cost analysis. A worked example and a case study follow. The case study compares their approach against Newton's method and Monte Carlo simulation, the standard method of averaging many random trials.
arxiv-2606-27075:
Bašić, Smajlović, and Šabanac study waves travelling on regular graphs, networks where every point has the same number of links. Their equation steps both space and time in discrete jumps, a forward time-difference scheme. An affine Laplace-type operator, a shifted measure of local unevenness, drives the motion. Two fundamental solutions, called wave kernels, describe how a single pulse spreads. The authors derive exact formulas for both kernels in this analysis of discrete propagation from 2026.

Kernel formulas rest on discrete modified Bessel functions plus counts of non-backtracking walks. Non-backtracking walks never reverse their last step, so they track genuine spreading paths. A uniqueness property of the kernel then yields a new trace-type formula for the operator. Examples include closed forms for trigonometric sums twisted by an additive character. Chebyshev polynomial sums weighted by binomial coefficients also get exact evaluations.
arxiv-2606-27275:
Levchenko asks why language models struggle with historical Italian, and breaks that struggle into distinct taxes. Her framework splits four costs: tokenization cost, predictive uncertainty, semantic robustness, and context sensitivity. Three datasets span three centuries, including a fresh corpus of seventeenth-century Italian digitised from page images. A canonical nineteenth-century novel serves as a high-exposure control, in a study published in 2026.

Encoding cost and comprehension come apart sharply. Older Italian and an eighteenth-century Russian stress test pay similar token penalties, roughly a quarter to a third more tokens. Predictive difficulty diverges: early Italian surprises models far more than its modern form, while Russian rises only modestly. Meaning embeddings stay robust across all sets, so models still represent old sense well. A minimal prompt giving temporal context cuts that surprisal by about sixty percent of its level.
arxiv-2606-27675:
Active galactic nuclei are bright galactic cores powered by black holes. Broad-line ones in the nearby southern sky lacked a complete spectroscopic census. Neelesh Amrutha and five colleagues present the OzSSy1 atlas in 2026 to supply it. The catalogue holds 887 broad-line active nuclei. All sit at redshift below zero point one, in the south and away from the galactic plane.

Observations came from the Wide Field Spectrograph on the Australian National University 2.3-metre telescope. Spectra were taken at resolving power near three thousand. The median signal-to-noise reached thirteen per angstrom in the blue arm and twenty-three in the red. Each spectrum carries a decomposition into nucleus and host galaxy light. Emission lines are fitted too, including broad hydrogen and helium components and forbidden oxygen, nitrogen, and sulphur lines. All data products are public, built to support population studies and variability work with future surveys.
arxiv-2606-27775:
A team including Csaba Balázs presents HydroGrav in 2026, a C++ code for cosmological phase transitions. First-order transitions in the early universe can source gravitational waves. Predicting the signal needs fluid profiles and wave spectra. HydroGrav builds self-similar fluid profiles from the exact equation of state. That equation comes directly from a model's effective potential. Bag-style equations are also supported.

A sound shell model inside the code computes the gravitational wave spectra. The team applies the framework to a Z2-symmetric extension of the Standard Model. The team compares fluid profiles and spectra from both treatments there. A scan across the model's parameter space maps where the treatments diverge. The scan also estimates the effect on signal-to-noise for LISA. Using the exact equation of state can shift detectability across the scanned space, the study finds.
arxiv-2606-28175:
A team including Xin Zhang presents HIcosmo, an open-source software framework for drawing conclusions about the universe from telescope and survey data. The framework targets the flood of data expected from next-generation sky surveys, which will deliver observations on a scale no earlier survey has matched.

HIcosmo is built on JAX, a library that computes derivatives automatically, so every step from model to likelihood to sampling can supply exact gradients. Zhang and colleagues checked it against reference codes: key values agreed closely, and final constraints differed by only a small fraction of the uncertainty. Sampling ran several times faster than a standard rival on ordinary processors, and far faster still on graphics hardware at survey scale.
arxiv-2606-28275:
Jihong Huang, Tommy Ohlsson, Sampsa Vihonen, and Shun Zhou apply quantum estimation theory to neutrino oscillations, the process by which neutrinos switch identity as they travel. The theory sets ultimate limits on how precisely any experiment could ever measure the oscillation parameters, whatever apparatus it uses.

Huang and colleagues first untangle a subtlety in the two-flavor case: the computed information depends on the chosen basis when the basis itself involves the unknowns. For three flavors they compute the full quantum Fisher information matrix for electron and muon neutrinos. Off-diagonal entries show the quantities are correlated, so fitting them together is not like fitting each alone. They convert the results into precision bounds for typical reactor and long-baseline accelerator experiments.
arxiv-2606-28375:
Yifan Liu, Shuang Miao, and Changhua Wei classify the fates of dust falling through a Schwarzschild black hole's spacetime. Their model is a pressureless fluid, dust, constrained to spherical symmetry, and classical solutions either persist forever or crash into a finite-time singularity where the density blows up.

Liu and colleagues sort the initial data into those two destinies, giving a complete criterion for which starting configurations evolve globally and which form singularities. For the singular cases they analyze the exact blowup profile, the detailed shape it takes as it approaches the singular time. Such sorting anchors the strict theory of gravitational collapse. Knowing the boundary between dispersal and blowup, and the profile at the boundary, guides both analysis and physical insight.
arxiv-2606-28475:
Seyed Farzad Bahreinian, Maziar Palhang, Mohammad Reza Taban, and Hasan Enami Eraghi attack a chronic failure of robot mapping. Simultaneous localization and mapping, where a robot charts its surroundings while tracking its own position, usually runs on an extended Kalman filter. Nonlinear motion and observation models force approximations whose errors can make the whole estimate diverge.

Bahreinian and colleagues add a simple compass and apply a carefully chosen transformation that rewrites the nonlinear state-space model as a genuinely linear one. The plain Kalman filter then applies exactly, giving their LMKF SLAM method. They report it significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods, especially extended-filter rivals, in accuracy, convergence, and computing cost, and stays steadier when sensor noise and system parameters vary. Experiments back the claims.
arxiv-2606-28775:
Yu, Lv, Wang, Wang and Xu put a photonic sampling device to work on a classic directed graph problem. Their device uses bipartite Gaussian boson sampling, where light passing through a circuit produces outcomes whose chances follow permanents, a matrix quantity suited to one-way connections. Most earlier sampling algorithms relied on a symmetric quantity tied to undirected problems, so directed cases were poorly served.

They define a task called Max-Perm as the natural target, and derive how much its sampling beats plain random choice in an ideal setting. Guided by those samples, a genetic algorithm then searches for a Hamiltonian cycle, a route visiting every node once in a directed graph. On random directed graphs the guided search beat a standard genetic algorithm. When no full cycle existed, it found longer valid paths, and tests showed the sampling-based start drove most of the gain.
arxiv-2606-28875:
Latifian and Rastegarzadeh present a way to estimate the energy of a cosmic ray from the radio flash its air shower produces. When a high-energy particle from space strikes the atmosphere, it creates a cascade of secondary particles that emits radio waves. Their method rests on CoREAS simulations, a standard simulation package, run for both the SURA experiment's antenna layout and a dense reference array of antennas.

Comparing simulated field strength between the two arrays yields a scale factor for each shower. That factor falls as the primary energy rises, giving a calibration curve for real events. Unlike earlier approaches, it barely depends on where the shower core lands. Reconstructing energies in tests gave a maximum error of about eleven percent, evidence the method is accurate and reliable.
arxiv-2606-28975:
Gamayun, Gritskov and Losev propose computing the conformal anomaly, a quantum breaking of scale symmetry, through cohomology, the algebraic study of obstructions. Their test case is a deformation of two-dimensional conformal field theories driven by a product of two currents, a standard exactly studied example. The anomaly's strength is captured by the beta function, which describes how a coupling changes with scale.

Using their approach, they reproduce the leading contribution of the well-known Cardy formula to the perturbative beta function. In their picture, that coefficient is the cocycle, an algebraic object realising the obstruction to deforming the state space's Virasoro module structure. The Virasoro algebra encodes these theories' symmetries. Beyond this reframing, the authors expect the method to become an efficient tool for higher-order beta function coefficients, where direct calculations grow painful.
arxiv-2606-29175:
Saito, Godsoe and Tan examine a gap in international humanitarian law opened by civilians using autonomous AI cyber systems. The law protects civilians unless they take direct part in hostilities. The Red Cross's 2009 guidance tests this with three criteria, one being direct causation: harm must follow in one causal step from the act.

That standard, the authors argue, fails for AI-mediated operations. When a civilian fields an autonomous multi-agent cyber system, harm comes from system decisions made after the human disengages. It is not one causal step away. The fallback integral-part test also fails, because it assumes downstream human contributors whose conduct can be classified. The framework thus treats such deployments as indirect participation, against its own purpose. The authors identify goal-specification granularity, how detailed the human's instructions are, as the hidden pivot of the test. They classify operations on a five-level spectrum.
arxiv-2606-29275:
Jain addresses a mismatch in diffusion language models: they are trained to denoise fixed sets of tokens, but at use time they must handle arbitrary configurations. Off the training grid, quality degrades. His method, Adaptive Block Diffusion, treats the configuration itself as random during training, optimising denoising risk across a spread of prefix and window layouts.

A single model then trains over the whole configuration space with no architectural change. Jain shows that generalisation across decoding strategies is governed by which configurations training covers, and that the method guarantees optimal denoising for any inference policy whose layouts were covered. In experiments the model stayed structurally stable across decoding scales, avoiding the off-grid collapse of fixed-block training. It also restored a clean pattern where larger blocks mean lower perplexity, and matched or beat fixed-block specialists at their own target scales.
arxiv-2606-29375:
Ji, Huang and Guo study how medical language models should size their adapters question by question. Models are commonly fine-tuned with LoRA, which adds a small low-rank adapter, using one fixed rank budget for every question. Yet medical questions differ in how confident the base model is, how well the training data covers their clinical area, and how hard cross-domain cases are.

Their system, TriageRA-CCF, is a teacher that supervises an adaptive budget router choosing a small, medium or large rank subset per question. Its three signals are computed solely from source training data, namely base-model answer confidence, clinical coverage of metadata cells, and a counterfactual near-miss score. Under a matched training protocol it topped LoRA, DoRA and MoELoRA baselines in average accuracy on two model families. The gains were modest and uneven, and ablations showed the three signals help, though not always together.
arxiv-2606-29975:
Ramlaoui and five colleagues present Atompack, a storage and distribution layer for atomistic machine learning datasets, the large collections of molecular records used to train models of materials and molecules. Training reads these immutable snapshots again and again in shuffled order.

Atompack is built for that workload: records are appended efficiently during construction, then an immutable index is committed and records are served whole through a memory-mapped read path. Against HDF5, LMDB, and ASE baselines, benchmarks cover sequential and shuffled reads, shared filesystems, write speed, and artifact size too. On a representative 64-atom workload, shuffled training-style reads run 96 times faster than the ASE LMDB baseline, with artifacts about 79 percent smaller.
arxiv-2606-30075:
Cecilia Erneman, Zeidan Zeidan, Göran Johansson, and Maryam Khanahmadi propose making flying cat-qubits on demand. Cat-qubits encode quantum information in superpositions of light states. Flying versions travel down a line to link distant quantum nodes. Usually such states are stored first, then released through a coupler. The authors instead generate and emit them in one process.

Time-dependent two-photon drives create the states directly from vacuum. The setting is a nonlinear bosonic system, such as a superconducting circuit. Two generation schemes are studied: Kerr-based and dissipation-based. During generation, the team shows logical control of the qubit is possible. The quantum information is shared between the system and the outgoing field. Photon loss and pure dephasing are both analyzed carefully. Generation and control stay robust under realistic noise levels. The work points toward programmable bosonic quantum networks.
arxiv-2606-30275:
Yuxuan Hu, Shihao Li, Yang Xiao, Gen Li, Feng Xu, and Jianfei Yang let a home robot actively aim its radar to read vital signs. Contact-free measurement of breathing and heart rate is hard at home. Millimeter-wave radar senses tiny chest motions through phase shifts. Radar only sees the radial part of any motion. Random robot and human orientations therefore destabilize the estimates.

Their framework, ActiveVital, treats sensing geometry as a control variable. Vision keypoints locate the chest anchor on the person's body. Alignment errors become steering commands for the robot. The radar moves toward near-normal incidence on the chest surface. A differential phase module further stabilizes the extracted signals. Breathing interval error drops from most of a second to a small fraction. Heart rate error falls from over thirteen beats to about two. Accuracy rivals controlled static sensing under messy home conditions.
arxiv-2606-30775:
Yangqiaoyu Zhou, Mohammad Alqudah, Kwei-Herng Lai and Aaron Halfaker report lessons from optimising the descriptions that route questions to an enterprise AI agent's skills. When two skills have overlapping descriptions, the routing model sends questions to the wrong skill, a failure the team call skill collision. With nine skills and three hundred seventy-two regression cases on a production chat agent, they built a pipeline to rewrite descriptions.

The pipeline's descriptions matched hand-tuned ones, at about seventy-nine percent F1 either way. Engineering effort per skill fell from two hours to under four minutes. Ablations on that system and on the ToolBench collection isolated the drivers. A single rewrite by a language model, fed any false-positive and false-negative cases, captured most of the gain. Iteration budgets, feedback composition, paired editing and training set size moved the score by under half a percent.
arxiv-2606-31075:
Wu and Feng settle a conjecture in extremal combinatorics. That field asks how large a structured family can be. The families here are sets of subsets. Any r of them must share at least one common element, so they are called r-wise intersecting families. Each element is included on its own, with its own probability, under a biased product measure. Tokushige had shown the largest such families are stars: sets that all contain one fixed element. His proof needed a restrictive hypothesis.

Tokushige conjectured the hypothesis could be weakened a lot. Wu and Feng prove the conjecture in full. Their key idea is a random partition method. It reduces the whole problem to at most r coordinates and solves those cases exactly. The method also covers cases where several coordinates are supercritical, too probable for earlier arguments to handle.
arxiv-2606-31175:
Neeraj and Sarkar report evidence that one meson leaves the fireball of a heavy-ion collision earlier than the rest. In lead-lead collisions at the LHC, a hot quark-gluon plasma expands and cools into ordinary hadrons. Kinetic freeze-out is the moment interactions stop. Whether every species freezes out together is an open question. The phi(1020) meson interacts weakly with other hadrons, so it may decouple early.

The authors fit the phi meson's momentum spectrum with a Boltzmann-Gibbs blast-wave model. They then compare its freeze-out point with the one shared by pions, kaons, and protons. In the most central collisions, the bulk freeze-out point is excluded at 4.1 sigma. Despite having a proton-like mass, the phi does not fit the bulk pattern. Its weak, OZI-suppressed interactions explain the early exit. Transport simulations with SMASH reproduce the effect.
arxiv-2606-31275:
Lefebvre and two colleagues present CLIMB, a memory system for learning from an endless unlabeled image stream. Online continual self-supervised learning must form good representations with no task boundaries and little storage. Older methods either replay stored examples or rely on regularisation alone to stop forgetting.

CLIMB joins both routes with a hierarchical centroid memory that groups similar images under cluster centres within a fixed budget. Those centres supply hard-to-tell-apart examples for contrastive learning and cover the spread of past data, while distillation on replayed items limits representation drift. On the Split CIFAR-100 and Split ImageNet-100 benchmarks, plus a new protocol with uneven task mixes, CLIMB beats leading methods in its class.
arxiv-2606-31375:
The ATLAS Collaboration measures how J/psi mesons, bound states of a charm quark and its antiquark, correlate with jets in proton and lead collisions. Charmonium yields are strongly suppressed in heavy-ion collisions by the quark-gluon plasma formed there. Reading that suppression needs a firm grip on how J/psi production relates to jet activity.

Using LHC data at 5.02 tera electron volts, the team separate prompt and non-prompt J/psi mesons and split them into isolated and jet-matched samples. Yields in lead-lead collisions, cross sections in proton-proton collisions, and nuclear modification factors are reported for each class. The matching uses small-radius jets rebuilt without the J/psi signal itself, so the accompanying jet activity is measured cleanly rather than assumed.
arxiv-2606-31475:
Hayward and two colleagues adapt rogue wave physics to spot the onset of extreme moves in financial volatility. Rogue waves in optics and water share statistical traits with volatility spikes, and both are hard to catch as they start. The team map volatility into a Schrödinger equation whose potential follows a Kerr nonlinearity.

They find signs of Anderson localisation, where waves trap in place, as a rogue peak nears in the VIX index. The slope of the system's smallest eigenvalue spikes reliably right at the onset of an extreme event. Simulated in real time, the method catches all but one major VIX peak, and out-of-sample tests on the VXO and VSTOXX repeat the feat. Early warning of market stress is the prize such a detector offers.
arxiv-2606-31775:
Hohn and six colleagues demonstrate energy-time entanglement from a single quantum dot grown directly on silicon. Quantum dots of III-V semiconductors are strong on-demand sources of entangled photons. Growing them on silicon, the standard manufacturing platform, has remained difficult. The dot here is InGaAs on GaAs, integrated monolithically with the substrate.

Under coherent two-photon excitation the team controls the biexciton-exciton cascade, shown by Rabi oscillations and dressed-state formation. A four-channel Franson interferometer records phase-dependent interference. Visibility reaches 64.0 percent with a stated uncertainty of seven points for short windows, approaching the Bell violation threshold. The result supports III-V-on-silicon dots as scalable sources for quantum photonics.
arxiv-2606-31975:
A team including Verner studies how the early universe reheats after inflation in no-scale supergravity models. In the minimal versions, the inflaton's decays into Standard Model fields are suppressed, just as decays into conformally coupled scalars are suppressed in the original Starobinsky model. Without efficient decays, the hot radiation era that follows inflation cannot begin on schedule.

Generalized models offer escape routes that the authors examine in turn. Changing the field-space curvature, as in string-derived variants, adding non-minimal gauge kinetic terms, or using anomaly-induced couplings can each restore inflaton decays. Direct and anomaly-induced couplings to gauge bosons and gauginos are analyzed, with the physical gauge coupling shown to be Kähler-frame invariant. Reheating temperatures and the resulting predictions for inflationary observables follow from each route.
arxiv-2608-00175: Inference-Time Policy Alignment for Fair Reinforcement Learning, arXiv 2608-00175. The fair RL. The paper remains available to readers. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources. The paper lived through the years.
arxiv-2608-00275: A Comparative Systems-Engineering Framework for RFI Coexistence in Radio Astronomy, arXiv 2608-00275. The RFI framework. Researchers may consult the paper. The file is now open to the public. Its contents inform the historical record. The library keeps the document safe.
awakening-to-the-real-1075: Awakening to the Real, 1075. The Taoist alchemical classic. This book preserves that text. The paper lasts as a quiet witness. Time has kept the file intact. The archive guards it with care. Those who study the era will use it.
cairnes-character-logical-method-1875:
John Elliott Cairnes published The Character and Logical Method of Political Economy in 1875. Cairnes, an Irish economist, was the friend and heir of John Stuart Mill. His book asks a basic question: what kind of science is economics, and how should it reason?

Cairnes defends the deductive method, which starts from known facts about human motives and argues toward conclusions. He answers the German historical school, which wanted economics rebuilt from case studies alone. The book also fixes the limits of the science, separating what economics can settle from what belongs to politics or morals. Clear and firm, it became the classic statement of classical method, read wherever economists argued about how their subject should work.
chanson-croisade-albigeoise-vol-1-1875:
The Chanson de la Croisade Albigeoise is a long poem in Old Provençal that tells the Albigensian Crusade as it happened, from 1209 onward. Two poets made it: a cleric who cheered the crusaders, and a second, nameless hand who took the side of Toulouse. Paul Meyer edited the text in 1875, and this is his first tome. The language is the tongue of the troubadours.

Sieges, burnings of heretics, the fall of Béziers and Carcassonne, and the death of kings crowd the verse. No other work lets readers hear the south of France speak of its own ruin. Meyer adds the apparatus of a modern edition to the old song. It is the crusade's great vernacular narrative.
childers-pali-dictionary-1875:
Robert Caesar Childers gave Pali studies their first dictionary in 1875, A Dictionary of the Pali Language, his life's work. Pali, the language of the oldest Buddhist canon, had few tools for English readers before his book appeared. Childers built entries from the texts themselves, with roots, forms, and citations drawn from scripture and commentary.

Every translator of the Pali canon since has stood on this groundwork, directly or through those it taught. The dictionary also spread knowledge of Buddhist terms and ideas far beyond the academy walls. Childers died young, in the year of publication, yet his single great book founded a field's daily practice in the West.
cia-0000008775:
One week in South Vietnam, April 8 to 14, 1965, fills a CIA situation report on military and political affairs. American Marines had landed at Da Nang the month before, and bombing of the north was under way. Saigon's government, meanwhile, kept changing hands.

Weekly reports stitched battlefield news to the capital's unstable politics in a single judgment. Policymakers used them to track whether the war effort was gaining or slipping. This week's entry catches the conflict at its great turning point, when American ground war began. Reading it now shows escalation judged day by day, not in hindsight.
cia-0000009975:
An American prisoner of war was sighted in Tay Ninh province, South Vietnam, a report dated January 1973 states. Tay Ninh, northwest of Saigon against the Cambodian border, had been a Viet Cong stronghold all war long. The date places the sighting in the ceasefire month itself.

A prisoner seen in the border province as peace began posed the usual hard alternatives. He might be awaiting release, hidden, or misreported altogether. The report entered the postwar files where such questions lived for years. This entry preserves the Tay Ninh claim at the moment the war's fighting formally stopped.
cia-0000010475:
Key problems facing American efforts to strengthen the Near East are listed in a March 1951 CIA paper. The Near East of the title runs from Egypt toward Pakistan in the usage of the time. Washington wanted a friendly barrier along the Soviet Union's southern edge.

The paper names the obstacles plainly: nationalism, weak states, Arab-Israeli conflict, and oil politics. Such candor helps readers see why the grand design kept failing. Alliance schemes drawn in Washington met a region pushing the other way. This early file states the mismatch at the start of a decade of trying.
cia-0000012275:
What a spy sends must be listed. An undated CIA document, its year estimated as 1961, inventories materials and documents to be sent in the Penkovsky case. The manifest belongs to the working file of the operation that ran Oleg Penkovsky, the Soviet colonel whose product filled whole shelves. Lists like this one kept track of a haul too valuable to handle loosely.

The inventory names the pieces of the colonel's product and the papers that moved with them. It shows clerks accounting for secrets with the care of bankers counting cash. For readers, the list is the case file's own catalog of its treasures.
cia-0000012375:
Joseph J. Bulik wrote to the chief of the Soviet Russia division in April 1963 about Oleg Penkovsky, and the memo opens the case's internal reckoning. The colonel had fallen silent the previous October, arrested in Moscow. Now the division that ran him began its post-mortem, asking the hard questions while the wounds were still fresh and the trial still ahead.

Such memos began the lessons-learned work every lost case demands. They weighed tradecraft, warning signs, and choices made under pressure. For readers, Bulik's page is the after-action's first draft: the lost asset assessed by the men who knew him best.
cia-0000013675:
Foreign Relations of the United States, 1961–1963, Volume XXII, covers Northeast Asia. It belongs to the State Department's official documentary series, FRUS. The volume prints the Kennedy years' diplomatic record for the region. It gathers cables, memos, and meeting notes on Japan, Korea, and the China questions. Department historians chose and declassified the pieces. The book sits in this file as the published face of the era's secret diplomacy.

The FRUS volumes are the diplomatic historian's bedrock sources. This one documents the New Frontier's handling of its Pacific allies and rivals. For readers, it offers the government's own record beside the secret estimates.
cia-0000013875: A captured American pilot was seen in Thanh Hoa Province back in January 1966, and a CIA note dated August 5, 1967, records the sighting. The report came well over a year after the event itself. Old sightings still counted, since they proved a man was alive on a known date. Each dated sighting helped close gaps in a prisoner's story.
cia-0000014775: A weekly meeting of the national executive board of Cuba's PSP fills a CIA file dated June 2, 1953. The file mentions politics the title clips mid word. Board meetings gave watchers the party's plans in near real time. This second Cuba board file in the set shows the steady rhythm of the watch.
cia-0000015275: An intense source of light was seen from the air, in a CIA file dated October 4, 1976. Aerial sightings came from trained crews, which gave them extra weight. A bright light with no clear source fit the classic pattern of these reports. The file keeps the crew's account in the agency's sky watch record.
cia-0000022775: Communist capabilities in Indochina are weighed in a CIA paper dated in 1954. That year France's war in Indochina ended at Dien Bien Phu and in Geneva talks. Judging what communist forces could do next shaped every plan for the region. The paper dates from the moment Vietnam was split and America's own long role there began.
cia-0000028175: Soviet preparations for the early launching of an earth satellite are reported in a CIA paper dated in 1957. In October that year Sputnik went up and stunned the American public. A paper on preparations, written as the launch neared, sits at the edge of that shock. It shows analysts reading the signs of a race their country was about to feel it had lost.
cia-0000037175:
A group of American prisoners was sighted in the northern part of the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, a CIA record dated June 3, 1981 reports. The northern region held the capital, Hanoi, and many wartime prison camps. Group sightings carried weight because they suggested organized detention, not strays.

The record preserves the sighting as another thread in the postwar search. Analysts compared its details with earlier reports from the same region. Standing alone it proved nothing. Joined with others, it helped draw the map of claims that investigators would spend the decade testing.
cia-0000042875:
El Salvador: Update 3 on Jesuit Killings is a CIA record dated January 2, 1990. The third numbered update followed the second within the same week. Fast numbering showed how closely the case was being tracked.

Inside, the probe's next steps are recorded in brief form. Brief updates favor facts over judgment, and this one is no exception to that useful rule. The series trusted the reader to draw the larger meaning from the dated facts. Names, hearings, and official statements make up its matter. The file's value is cumulative: set between updates two and four, it keeps the chronicle unbroken for anyone tracing the case today.
cia-0000044475:
General Ponce provided a list of soldiers near the site of the killings, in a CIA record dated January 4, 1990. The site was the university residence where the priests were murdered. A list from the army's own chief marked a formal step.

Inside, the roster of soldiers is handed over and preserved. Names near a crime scene are where investigations properly begin. The general's act could be read as candor or as control. Either way, the file marks the point at which the army's own paper began to name its men in the case that would define it.
cia-0000045275: Armed men holding municipal officials in El Salvador failed to free them as expected, and a CIA report dated September 6, 1985, records the letdown. The item comes from the daily flow of reporting on the civil war, when kidnappings of local officials were common news. One small episode survives here: men taken, a release looked for, and no release made.
cia-0000045875: A Japanese source claimed in 1989 that American prisoners of war were still held in Vietnam. A CIA item dated May 3, 1989, filed the report. SRV, the Socialist Republic of Vietnam, was Hanoi's formal name for the reunified country. Claims like this one kept the missing-men issue alive long after the war, and each one had to be checked.
cia-0000046075: Hanoi announced that a third F-111 had been brought down, and a CIA item dated October 2, 1972, kept the claim. The F-111 was a swing-wing bomber then flying some of the air war's hardest missions. Each claimed loss was checked in Washington against what American records showed. The claims were also a weapon in themselves.
cia-0000049075: A Salvadoran held in Honduran custody drew a CIA trace in 1983, kept with the Truth Commission records. Prisoners across borders raised questions neither government liked to answer in writing. The trace follows one captive on paper, through the hands of two states at war's edge. The file keeps the questions open.
cia-0000049175: A New York Times article on the Jesuit case, partly blacked out, survives in a CIA item from 1990. The Times's coverage carried the murders' story to the audience that funded the war: the American public and its Congress. The clipping sits in the Truth Commission files, its hidden lines marking what stayed secret.
cia-0000049275: House members Beilenson, Glickman, and McHugh were briefed in 1989, on Nicaragua and the region around it, and a CIA item preserves the session. Three members at once made it a small seminar, the kind where votes on Central America were quietly formed. The record sits among the Truth Commission files' congressional paper.
cia-0000049375: New killings plaguing the government in El Salvador form the subject of declassified CIA document 0000049375, dated October 5, 1987. The item carries a Truth Commission note and centers on fresh killings as a problem for the government. Readers get a brief declassified record whose heading gives its whole point, preserved as filed in the agency's Salvadoran reporting.
cia-0000096475: British Guiana is the whole title of declassified CIA document 0000096475, dated October 1, 1964. The single place name gives no topic beyond the territory itself. Readers get a brief declassified country item whose generality stands out. It is one of several British Guiana records in the catalog. They come from the colony's final years as a named territory.
cia-0000096975: Cuban promise to Bolivian exiles to step up the pace of revolutionary activity is the first numbered item in declassified CIA document 0000096975, dated October 3, 1967. The heading numbers the item, suggesting a list. Readers get a short declassified record of a promise from Cuba to exiles, preserved as one entry among the agency's Bolivia-era filings.
cia-0000098275: Anti-Mao Activity in Southern Yunnan Province is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000098275, dated October 5, 1968. The heading names opposition activity and one southern province. Readers get a short declassified provincial item from China reporting, filed months after the neighboring Kunming record on tension and disrupted daily life in the same province.
cia-0000098575: Special National Intelligence Estimate on foreign reactions to certain U.S. courses of action, in shortened heading form, is declassified CIA document 0000098575, dated January 5, 1967. The heading leaves the courses themselves unspecified. Readers get a formal estimate record on how others might react, a companion in type to the Dominican stability estimate.
cia-0000102975:
South Korea: USSR Won't Discuss Sakhalin Koreans with Japan is declassified CIA document 0000102975, dated May 1, 1983. The sample is a Korea Herald report, carried in English in June 1983. It quotes Prime Minister Yasuhiro Nakasone on the Soviet refusal to treat returning Koreans as a topic for talks with Japan.

Since 1975, the Soviet Union had allowed only three Koreans to leave Sakhalin for Japan, the report says. Japan was willing to accept all 438 Koreans who had applied for entry permits there. The Soviet Union had also refused a Japanese request to investigate the conditions under which Koreans lived in Sakhalin.
cia-0000106275: Communist Road Development in Laos is the subject of declassified CIA document 0000106275, dated November 4, 1965. The heading tracks road building by communist forces inside Laos. Roads are the stated subject, rather than troops or battles, in the title itself. The brief record is an infrastructure item from the secret war period in Laos, dated late in 1965.
cia-0000108075: American and Thail Prisoners Near Ban Na Kay in Houa Phan Province is the heading, with Thai misspelled, on declassified CIA document 0000108075, dated October 4, 1966. The title places American and Thai prisoners near one named place in Laos. Ban Na Kay and Houa Phan Province are both named in full. The brief record preserves the misspelling exactly as released.
cia-0000108475: Weekly Situation Report on International Terrorism - 23 July 1980 is the heading on declassified CIA document 0000108475, dated May 1, 1980. The title dates its week to July 23, 1980, well after the May file date. That gap stands on the face of the record itself. The brief record is one weekly issue in a long terrorism series from 1980.
cia-0000119675: Untitled CIA record from February 1969 holding a statement by John Sweeney. Nothing in the heading says who Sweeney was or why his words were taken down. The file keeps his statement as it was recorded for the agency. Untitled statements of this kind were usually raw material, a person's own words taken down for the file rather than a finished study.
cia-0000124275: Dated November 1957, this CIA item notes the announcement of the earth satellite launching at a Soviet embassy reception, the date in the heading breaking off. Moscow unveiled its triumph to diplomats in a social setting. The item captures that rollout as the agency heard of it. Embassy receptions doubled as listening posts in the Cold War, and a launch announced over drinks became a reportable event for every service watching that room.
cia-0000126875: From August 1968, a CIA report gathers reaction across the Third World to the Soviet invasion of Czechoslovakia. Newly free nations had just watched a superpower crush a smaller state. The paper collects their responses, which ran from anger to silence to cold calculation. Third World answers were tallied because the invasion landed in the middle of the contest for the new nations, whose votes and ports both blocs wanted.
cia-0000126975: An October 1975 CIA Weekly Review covers Angola under the heading After Independence. Formal independence was a month away, and civil war among the rival movements was already under way. The review looks at what came next as Portugal prepared to leave. The review's timing is its irony. Independence day fell on November 11 that year, and the after in its heading already meant a country at war with itself.
cia-0000132275: Situation Report 581 belongs to the CIA's Iraq-Kuwait series. Dated January 1, 1991, it covers political developments. Its headline tells of bombs exploding in a place whose name is cut off in the record title. The report deals with bombings tied to the Gulf crisis but happening far from the Gulf itself. Readers get a short crisis update whose sharpest detail, the location, survives only in the full text.
cia-0000132575: A boundary dispute between Peru and Ecuador fills a CIA document dated October 1, 1960. The headline shortens Peru to Pru, a slip kept from the original. The two Andean neighbors had argued over their border for a century and fought a war over it in 1941. That war settled little in the end. The short document covers the dispute's state in 1960.
cia-0000132675: Rebel work growing inside Cuba fills a CIA paper dated March 4, 1961. Its headline misspells activity as activitty, a slip kept from the original. The anti-Castro underground was growing bolder month by month that spring. Its members hoped the coming invasion would tip the balance in their favor. The short paper tracks the rise in raids, plots, and arrests.
cia-0000132775: An August 4, 1960 entry in the Cuban Developments series, this CIA paper was filed as a companion to another same-day entry. Exile training was under way by then, and the United States was committed to action against Castro. Both entries continue the summer series. The declassified text survives through the CIA Reading Room mirror at the Internet Archive.
cia-0000134275: Castro's harsh acts driving away other Latin American states fill a CIA paper dated October 4, 1959. The region's democrats were recoiling from the violence of the revolution's first year. Trials, firing squads, and seized property were costing Havana friends month by month. The short paper tracks that loss of goodwill and the acts that caused it.
cia-0000135875: 4 October 1953 is the date on a declassified CIA planning paper about the program for PBSUCCESS, the phased plan the 1954 coup would later follow. The wider file is PBSUCCESS, the CIA operation aimed at the Arbenz government in Guatemala before the June 1954 coup. The heading alone tells a reader the topic, the channel, and the moment, even where names stay deleted.
cia-0000135975: The cable dated 6 January 1954 in the CIA files, now open, deals with detected surveillance of a residence, watchers spotted around a house the operation used. The name Lincoln marks the forward station of PBSUCCESS, the CIA campaign that brought down President Arbenz in June 1954. The paper trail here is small but direct, a single piece of the huge file the operation left behind.
cia-0000136275: Dated 1 May 1954, a declassified CIA cable deals with broadcast tape production, the factory floor of the radio station and its daily output. Lincoln handled the field traffic of PBSUCCESS, the agency effort against the Arbenz government in Guatemala in the early 1950s. For readers of the coup, the value lies in the plain wording, written before anyone knew how the story would end.
cia-0000136375: Money for the new government is the subject of this July 1954 LINCOLN cable on immediate funding requirements. It is impossible to estimate funds remaining in CALLIGERIS's hands, the station admits, because the organization is broke and his receipts were never fully accounted. A PBSUCCESS budget estimate of 750,000 dollars for the period after 7 July was approved, plus 200,000 sent as a special fund. The cable recommends releasing 405,000 dollars at once to liquidate liberation army debts and pay families of the war dead.
cia-0000136875: Headquarters backs the LCFLUTTER team flight plan in this March 1954 cable. The travel rules are pure clandestine craft. Team members stay in different hotels. They meet only at the team point. Each man knows the other only by alias. One man will depart in April. The job can be done in both target areas by May, he estimates. Headquarters asks for more detail. It wants the black travel plan spelled out. It also asks whether the aircraft type is adequate.
cia-0000136975: Use the wire-service text, not the true text. Headquarters gives that advice to LINCOLN in May 1954. The subject is Molotov's reply to an appeal for assistance. Hours were spent on a London-datelined dispatch. It quotes Radio Moscow on Molotov's promise. The quoted language is garbled in this copy. The point survives anyway. For propaganda use, the press version served better than the verified original. Headquarters wanted the field to run with it.
cia-0000139475: A third 1986 report from the DCI's hostage location task force is preserved as document 0000139475. The task force existed because Americans were being seized and held in Beirut and elsewhere, and finding them fell in part to intelligence work. Its reports weighed sightings, sources, and guesses about hidden holding sites. The record for this item names no captive and no place. The file is best taken as one installment in a series that tracked a crisis Washington could not solve by force.
cia-0000141175:
Celina Romero de Gonzalez filed a death claim with the U.S. Department of Labor in March 1969 for her son, Juan Gonzalez Romero. The form says he died on 17 April 1961. That was the first day of the Bay of Pigs landing in Cuba, the CIA-run operation in which Cuban exile air crew flew and died. The claim names her as his mother and lists his brother Modesto among kin.

Forms like this one were the slow paper tail of the failed landing. Years after the event, a mother in Cuba had to state dates, kin, and facts of birth so the U.S. government could judge her claim for death benefits tied to secret work.
cia-06795975: Chernobyl's meltdown cost the Soviet economy dearly. This CIA study tallied the nuclear accident's economic fallout. The price of disaster, calculated. Its contents inform the historical record. This file preserves that declassified assessment. Kept for readers.
